World.title: In rural Chad, solar kiosks bring healthcare closer
World.content:
Bitkine, Chad – For Ache Kodo, seeing a doctor once meant saving money for the journey.

Living in Bitkine, in central Chad, she said a medical visit could mean paying for transport, the consultation and other costs of travelling to a larger town.

Now, she can consult a doctor remotely through a Telemedan kiosk closer to home.

“Telemedan changed how my family accessed healthcare services,” Ache told Al Jazeera. “It was difficult before, as it involved me saving money to travel just to see a doctor. Now I’m able to do it on time with fewer costs from where I am. It has also enhanced my economic status.”

For people in rural Chad, distance can be as much of a barrier to healthcare as the shortage of doctors themselves. Medical facilities and specialists are concentrated in larger towns and cities, leaving many communities far from basic services.

Abakar Mahamat grew up with that reality.

“The problem wasn’t only the lack of doctors,” he said. “It was also the distance between those doctors and the communities that needed them.”

In 2021, he launched Telemedan, a telemedicine initiative designed to bring consultations closer to communities where electricity, internet access and medical infrastructure are limited.

“Instead of asking people to travel hundreds of kilometres to find a doctor, I wanted to use technology to bring the doctor closer to them,” Abakar told Al Jazeera.



A clinic powered by the sun

The kiosks run on solar panels and batteries, allowing them to operate without reliable grid electricity.

A local operator registers the patient and takes basic measurements using equipment including blood-pressure monitors, glucometers, thermometers, pulse oximeters and electrocardiogram (ECG) machines.

The doctor joins remotely, appearing on a screen as the operator assists with the examination.

Telemedan says its kiosks can also be equipped with diagnostic tools including stethoscopes, temperature sensors and, in some cases, ultrasound equipment. A trained local operator helps patients use them.

The system is designed for places where internet access may be unreliable. Patient information can be stored locally and synchronised when connectivity returns. An Unstructured Supplementary Service Data (USSD) service allows people without internet access to book appointments and access health information.

Depending on the location, the kiosks can connect through mobile networks or satellite links.

“We want to see that the absence of reliable electricity or the internet should not mean the absence of healthcare,” Abakar said.

The cost of getting to a doctor

Abakar said some journeys for medical care can cost $200 or more once transport, accommodation, logistics and medical consultations are included.

Telemedan consultations cost between $2 and $15, depending on the service.

For Abakar, the issue is also about what families can afford to give up to obtain care.

“A patient should not have to choose between seeking medical care and being able to feed their family,” he said.

From pilot to wider network

Telemedan began as a pilot and has expanded with support from grants and institutional partnerships, including Chad’s Ministry of Public Health and Prevention.

Abakar said the initiative now has 37 kiosks across 11 provinces and has reached an estimated 143,000 people.

Telemedan has also begun using artificial intelligence to help screen for diabetic retinopathy, a complication of diabetes that can damage vision. The initiative says the technology is intended to assist healthcare professionals rather than replace them.



But a remote consultation has limits.

A kiosk cannot provide emergency treatment or perform every examination. Patients who need specialist care, laboratory tests, medicines or hospital treatment still have to reach the next level of the health system.

Can the kiosks last?

Telemedan’s expansion comes as Chad develops its wider digital health system.

Youssouf Silay, an assistant to the coordinator of Chad’s National Digital Health Programme, told Al Jazeera that the country’s National Health Development Plan for 2022–2030 identifies digital health as a way to expand access to care.

Chad established the National Telemedicine Programme in 2021 and launched its National Digital Health Programme in 2023, Youssouf said. The Ministry of Health is also developing a legal and regulatory framework for digital health services.

“The objective is to promote innovative solutions that can improve access to healthcare, particularly in areas with limited medical and energy infrastructure,” Youssouf told Al Jazeera. “Solutions such as solar-powered telemedicine kiosks can contribute to this effort by bringing healthcare services closer to underserved populations.”

But putting a kiosk in a village is only the beginning.

The equipment has to keep working. Connectivity has to be available. Local operators need training. Doctors need to be there when patients call. And people who need care beyond the kiosk need a way to reach it.

Each kiosk costs about $10,000, according to Abakar. Telemedan sells the units to governments, public health programmes and partner organisations, which then operate them. The model means patients are not paying for the infrastructure itself.

Telemedan says it wants to reach one million people in rural communities across sub-Saharan Africa.

A solar-powered kiosk cannot replace a hospital. It cannot replace a doctor in every circumstance.

But it can shorten the distance between a patient and the health system.

“We want Telemedan to become a sustainable layer of healthcare infrastructure, not simply a collection of technology projects,” Abakar told Al Jazeera.

World.title: Canada to hit US with retaliatory tariffs as trade war escalates
World.content:
Mark Carney says Canada will impose tariffs starting September 8 on imports of US steel, electronics and other products.

Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced retaliatory tariffs on the United States after Washington imposed a 50 percent levy on $20bn worth of Canadian goods.

Carney, speaking in Ottawa on Saturday, said the new Canadian tariffs would target US steel, dairy and electronics industries among others and take effect on September 8.

“Canada will match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses,” Carney told reporters.

The announcement came after days of intense negotiations broke down late on Friday, worsening a delicate relationship between the longtime trade partners and allies.

US President Donald Trump’s new tariffs hit sectors including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing rods and hockey equipment, and cover some $20bn worth of goods, or 5.5 percent of Canadian exports to the US.

Trump responded to Carney’s announcement saying “Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!” He claimed Canada has also charged US farmers “massive amounts” of tariffs for years, and added, “No more!!!”

Carney is one of the few global leaders to retaliate against US tariffs and has pledged to forge new trade and military alliances, despite Canada’s dependence on the ‌US for nearly 70 percent of its exports.

In Ottawa on Saturday, Carney said the talks with the US broke down after Trump set conditions that were ultimately unacceptable even though earlier talks had been positive.



“In recent days, the United States proposed new terms that were uneconomic, unfair and undermined the net benefits for Canada, and called into question the reliability of any deal,” Carney said, adding these demands included curtailing Canada’s ability to forge new trade deals.

“We cannot accept what they’ve offered, and we will not give what they’ve asked.”

He added that US negotiators also made unacceptable “threats” to the French language and “Quebec culture”, referring to the French-speaking province in eastern Canada.

Canada to target US steel and diary industries

He said Canada will impose tariffs on US steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics, along with some products the US previously targeted in Canada. The government will release details on its response in the coming days, he said.

He added that Canada would announce support measures next week for industries hit ⁠by the new US duties, adding these measures could last years.

The new US tariffs are expected to have a major impact on Canada’s economy.

“Costs are going to go up, prices are going to go up, unemployment is going to go up as well,” said Al Jazeera’s David Mercer, reporting from the Canadian city of Calgary. “And it’s been warned that business owners – small [and] medium-sized businesses – some of those will have to declare bankruptcy,” he said.

At the same time, Mercer said, Carney is selling the trade war as an opportunity for Canada to strengthen its trade relations with other countries.

“He’s been around the world, he’s been talking to countries in Asia, in Europe, shoring up new trade relationships, wanting to diversify Canada’s economy and Canada’s trade relationships with other countries around the world just to get away from that dependency that Canada has traditionally had on the United States,” he said.

Public opinion surveys in Canada show most Canadians back a “tougher approach” to the US in the trade talks. A poll by Leger last week said 56 percent of Canadians favoured a hard line and making no more concessions.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, one of the most vocal ⁠opponents of US tariffs, supported Carney’s decision to retaliate.

“I’m glad he didn’t sign that deal because it was a bad deal. It was a bad deal for Ontario. It was a bad deal for the auto sector, the steel sector, and manufacturing sector,” Ford told reporters on Saturday.

‘Only realistic next step’

In Port Colborne, Ontario, resident Stuart Edwards said the trade war was going to “hurt everybody” and “it’s just sad”.



“We have a bully in Washington, and he’s just hitting us all with the big stick all the time,” he said. “And we’re not going to put up with it; Canada isn’t. We’ll fight back.”

But Pamela Coulis, from Fort Erie in Canada, was worried about rising prices.

“I think probably the gas will go up even more, and all products, from food to, I don’t know, wood, everything else,” she said.

Diamond Isinger, who served as a special adviser to former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, said both countries will suffer from the trade war.

“It’s going to cause pain and challenge for Canadians and Americans alike – in terms of the actions that, unfortunately, the US has taken as well as Canada’s retaliation. But ultimately this was the way forward; this was the only realistic next step,” she said.

“Because the US administration responds best, of all the responses that they could have, to all the actions that a government like Canada could take, to strength,” Isinger added.

“So, we could not simply accept 50 percent tariffs going forward. We had to move forward with our own retaliatory package.”

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told Fox News on Saturday that no new ⁠talks are planned with Canada.

“We’re moving forward with measures that respond to Canadian retaliation,” Greer said. “They’ve always had the best deal, and they still would have an even better deal, but they didn’t want that.”

The escalating trade war meanwhile has been met with anger by Democratic lawmakers and governors from border states including Minnesota, New York and Washington, who blamed Trump for triggering chaos that would raise costs for US businesses and families.

“Needlessly picking fights with our allies and raising prices here at home. That’s Trump’s economic policy in a nutshell,” New York Governor Kathy Hochul posted on X.

The Business Roundtable, a group of 200 chief executives of leading US corporations, also warned the new tariffs “risk raising costs for American businesses and families”, and urged both governments to resume negotiations.

World.title: Carney says Trump started trade war with fresh tarrifs 'attack'
World.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney has said a fresh wave of US tariffs on Canada is a "miscalculation" designed to "hurt and divide us", after trade talks collapsed late on Friday.

"They asked too much and they offered too little," Carney said on Saturday, adding that that the US and Canada were now in a trade "war". "You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked," he said.

The prime minister confirmed he would match US tariffs "dollar-for-dollar" from 8 September, including levies on steel, dairy, appliances and electronics.

The collapse of the trade talks upends a deeply integrated trading relationship, with no clear path to resolution. US President Donald Trump has yet to comment.

"We cannot accept what they've offered, and we will not give what they've asked," Carney said.

Both countries were optimistic of a deal earlier in the week, but talks fell apart after both sides accused the other of making last-minute changes.

Now that talks have broken down, Canada has been hit with new 50% US tariffs on a range of Canadian goods, in addition to existing US tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminium, automobiles and lumber.

The new tariffs are limited in scope, covering about $20bn (Â£15bn; C$28bn) of Canadian imports, or about 5% in total, including wine, dairy, cement, clothing and hockey equipment.

The prime minister said Canada was retaliating "reluctantly" to protect its interests. Details of the counter-measures will be released in the coming days, he said.

Leaders of other federal parties in Canada, including the Conservative opposition, voiced support for the prime minister, as have the leaders of some Canadian provinces.

Tariffs - a tax placed on imports from other countries - have been a key component of Trump's trade policy, with the US president arguing they will boost American manufacturing and create jobs at home.

Critics, however, say tariffs have raised prices for American consumers and have disrupted and damaged the global economy.

World.title: Carney faces crucial test after walking away from Trump's deal
World.content:
The United States and Canada have entered into uncharted territory.

The longtime allies and economic partners, who have enjoyed free trade for decades, are now in an escalating trade war with no clear off ramp.

And for Prime Minister Mark Carney, the late night decision to suspend talks with President Donald Trump and to retaliate instead of agreeing to a deal that seemed in reach will be a significant political test.

He is one of the first world leaders to walk away from the negotiating table with the White House - and the outcome will be closely watched.

Both sides have blamed last-minute changes for torpedoing the tentative deal, with Carney saying the US "asked too much" and "offered too little".

Carney's decision will challenge the appetite among Canadians to accept some economic pain as Ottawa pushes for more US concessions.

After rejecting Trump's high pressure tactics, and in choosing to hit back against the latest duties, Carney will need to convince Canadians that the economic pain is worth the cost of standing up to the Trump administration in search of a better agreement in the long run.

In remarks on Saturday, he said "we take this step confident this is in the best interest of Canada" and accused the US of a "power play" by seeking eleventh-hour changes.

Asked by a reporter whether the US and Canada were locked in a trade war, he replied: "You're at war when you're attacked - we got attacked."

Switching to French, he said the spiralling trade dispute "wasn't our choice", adding: "Canada is strong, Canada is ready, Canada is united."

There is no doubt this will cause pain on both sides of the border, with business facing more pressure from US duties and Canadian counter-tariffs.

Canada sends about 70% of its exports to the US, and the country is the top trading partner for a number of US states, with Michigan, Kentucky, Indiana and Ohio among the most exposed.

Carney came to power with a call for "elbows up" - an ice-hockey term for an aggressive approach - vowing to fight for Canada in the face of a Trump administration keen to exert economic pressure for its America First agenda.

Many Canadians have told pollsters that they are willing to fight.

A recent survey by Abacus Data suggested that around 36% of Canadians would support retaliating to US tariffs, while a Leger poll indicated that 56% of Canadians want the federal government to take a hard line and make no more concessions.

Canadians frustrated with the US tariffs have already chosen to avoid travelling there. The boycott has meant a loss of about C$3.3bn ($2.35bn; Â£1.75bn) in travel revenue for the US last year.

A decision by most provinces to remove US alcohol from store shelves has hammered that sector.

Based on US government trade data, US wine exports to Canada fell 78% year over year, a $357m loss in export value. The US distillers association reported similar numbers - saying provincial bans have caused exports of American spirits to drop by more than 70%.

The ban quickly became a point of frustration for the Trump administration.

Canadaâs prime minister will also need to convince the provinces who have been less affected by the US trade dispute so far that walking away is a risk worth taking.

He briefed them on Saturday on the current state of affairs, and for now, they are showing a united front.

British Columbia Premier David Eby said he was committed to the "national project we are on", while Ontario Premier Doug Ford said "we didn't start this fight but I can assure you, we're going to win this fight".

World.title: Rescuers dig through Ukraine mall wreckage as Zelensky condemns 'despicable' Russian strike
World.content:
Rescuers in Ukraine are continuing their search for survivors in the wreckage of a big shopping centre hit by Russia on Friday.

Sixteen people were killed and 130 injured when two drones hit the busy centre in Kryvyi Rih in quick succession in what is known as a double-tap strike. Four people are still missing. The search and rescue operation could last for another two days.

President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned the "cynical and despicable" attack in which the second drone targeted emergency workers.

The sides exchanged more fire overnight, with Ukrainian attacks said to have killed at least four people in Russia, including two children, and three people reported dead by Kyiv as a result of Russian strikes.

The death toll from Friday's attack reached 16 after another body was retrieved from the rubble overnight, said Dnipropetrovsk regional head Oleksandr Hanzha.

"We're doing everything possible to speed up... the search and rescue operation," he told Ukrainian TV on Saturday morning.

He added that the work could continue for another two days because of the sheer scale of devastation and constant threats of more Russian attacks.

Rescue teams from seven other Ukrainian regions were urgently deployed on Friday evening to help search for survivors.

The huge fire covering an area of some ââ9,000 sq m has been extinguished.

In an update later on Saturday, Hanzha said that 52 injured people, including 14 children, were still in city hospitals.

Dozens of people had already undergone surgery, said Kryvyi Rih's miltiary chief Oleksandr Vilkul.

A day of mourning is being observed across the Dnipropetrovsk region.

Dramatic footage verified by the BBC showed the second drone hitting the already burning shopping centre in Zelensky's hometown. Russia's military has not commented.

Vilkul said the drones had been flying at "extremely low altitudes" and described the attackers as "animals".

Officials have not commented on why Ukraine's air defence units - which the military says are 90% successful at intercepting drones - failed to stop Friday's attacks on the shopping centre.

Ukraine's interception rate of ballistic missiles, however, is much lower - at about 40%, the defence ministry reported in June. Kyiv has repeatedly said it is running low on US-made Patriot missiles - the most effective weapon against the ballistics.

The attack in Kryvyi Rih came a day after 17 people were killed and more than 40 injured in a major Russian missile and drone attack on Ukraine's capital Kyiv.

World.title: Father leaves 7-year-old son alone on Mount Fuji to continue hike
World.content:
A father has been reprimanded by police after leaving his son on Japan's highest mountain for several hours with just a soft drink and snack.

The seven-year-old was spotted sitting on a bench on Mount Fuji in foggy and rainy conditions, at a point situated at over 2,000m (6,500ft).

His father, 48, reportedly told him to "wait here" after the boy complained he was tired - and continued the climb with his elder son.

Staff at a mountain hut found the child near the sixth station of a hiking route towards the summit and alerted police. His father was tracked down between the route's seventh and eighth stations - said to be a three-hour hike away.

The boy was found on his own at 07:30 local time on Thursday (22:30 GMT).

Officers castigated his father when he returned from the higher station and reunited with his son, who is said to have been "tired and fussy" after eight hours of waiting.

"Even if it means having to give up on climbing the mountain together, leaving a child behind is unacceptable," one told him, according to Japan Today. He is said to have apologised for the "rash" decision.

The family was reported to have been on the Fujinomiya route, which starts from the fifth station on the mountain, a spot which is accessible by public transport.

From there it takes around five hours to reach the peak and a further three hours to get down, climbing guides suggest.

World.title: Syria says Israeli strike near Damascus violation of international law
World.content:
Syria has condemned an Israeli attack on the village of Beit Jinn, southwest of the country's capital Damascus, which officials said hit a civilian vehicle and left several people injured.

The attack was the second known Israeli strike on Syria in the past week, with Syria branding it a "violation" of its sovereignty and international law.

In a post on X, the Israeli military said it had targeted a "terrorist" in the "final stages" of preparing attacks which posed an immediate threat to soldiers.

The latest incident comes days after reports emerged Israel had struck a military airbase close to the Turkish border, which Syria said threatened to escalate tensions in the region.

After the earlier attack, Washington issued a rare rebuke of Israel, calling it an "unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability".

In an interview on Friday, the US ambassador to Turkey, Tom Barrack, suggested that the strike could be "the Israelis baiting the Turks" in an attempt to draw Turkey into a conflict ahead of upcoming Israeli elections.

Barrack's comments led Israel's far-right defence minister, Israel Katz, to describe his account as "full of inaccuracies".

Writing on X, Katz added Israeli forces were acting "in light of clear intelligence information about Turkey's intentions".

Following Tuesday's strikes on the Abu al-Duhur airbase, the office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu published a statement: "Israel and Syria agreed to a status quo in security matters, which Syria was on the verge of breaching by permitting Turkish troops to deploy at an airbase near Aleppo."

World.title: 'We're not going to run from it': Sydney Marathon laughs off medal error
World.content:
Recognisable Sydney landmarks feature on the double-sided medal, including the Opera House and Harbour Bridge, which are part of the 42.2km (26.2 mile) course.

Users on social media noticed the shape of the stadium engraved on the medal appeared to be carved in the wrong likeness.

Munich's Allianz Arena is sculpted by thousands of diamond-shaped inflatable cushions, while Sydney's similarly named Allianz Stadium has a flatter facade smoothed with long bronze fins.

Sydney Marathon confirmed runners would receive the medal depicting the incorrect city's stadium, noting: "It's a beautiful medal, and now a little more unique."

"It's certainly given everyone something to talk about this weekend, mostly in good humour."

Germany's Allianz Arena also poked fun at the mistake, writing on Instagram: "Oh wow, we didn't have that on our bingo card!"

"Perhaps they tried to find something else they had in common: Allianz Arena -- Sydney Opera -- Unique Architecture -- Both are worth a visit!"

The reverse side of the Sydney Marathon medal shows a gold and indigo pattern designed by First Nations artist Ambrose Killian, widely commended for its ornate pattern.

He confirmed to the BBC that he was not involved in designing the other face of the medal engraved with the wrong stadium.

Some 40,000 runners will take part in the event on 30 August, following more than 120,000 ballot entries.

Organisers praised record participation and fundraising for this year's event.

World.title: Swedish sword attack victim was 17-year-old girl, police say
World.content:
The victim of a deadly sword attack at a high school in central Sweden was a 17-year-old girl, police have confirmed.

Two boys aged 12 and 17 were also seriously injured in the attack at Brinell School in Fagersta on Friday afternoon, according to local authorities, while a third person sustained minor injuries.

An 18-year-old man, who has not been named, was arrested and police said they were treating the case as murder and attempted murder.

Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson and opposition leader Magdalena Andersson visited the school, where flower tributes have been laid to honour the victims, on Saturday morning.

Students at the school had only just returned to the classroom following the summer break when the deadly attack unfolded on Friday afternoon.

The police later confirmed they fired shots after being called to the scene but did not say whether the alleged attacker was hit before he was detained.

Sweden's public broadcaster reported that the suspect was wearing a helmet. Local media also said he was a former student.

The region went into a state of emergency on Friday, but it had ended by Saturday.

The school has just under 500 students on its roster, according to SVT, and is located 170km (105 miles) north-west of the capital, Stockholm.

Investigators have already carried out two house searches in connection with the suspect, police said.

On Friday, Sweden's Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson described the attack as a "serious incident," and said "we do not know what lies behind the act, but we know that police are working very intensively", in a post on X.

Sweden's King Carl XVI Gustaf said he received the news "with dismay and sadness".

World.title: Fourteen killed in strike on Myanmar monastery
World.content:
Fourteen people were killed in military air strikes at a monastery in Myanmar early on Friday, opposition fighters and a local rescue worker have said.

All of those killed were elderly and a number of monks were also injured, the rescue worker told BBC Burmese, adding that the site was struck twice.

The attack happened at around 09:00 local time (02:30 GMT) in Myaung township in the central Sagaing region, some 70km (47 miles) west of Mandalay, the news agency AFP reported.

Civilians had reportedly gathered at the site for a meditation retreat to mark Buddhist Lent. Myanmar's military has not commented.

Nway Oo Myaung, a pro-democracy rebel, told AFP that the victims included 11 men and three women. Five of the victims were said to be from one village, while the remaining nine were from a neighbouring township.

"Older people had entered the meditation centres," Myaung added, saying the dead were aged between 50 and 70.

A second, unnamed opposition fighter said he had been among those searching for survivors of the attacks.

"While we were trying to rescue people, the aircraft came to bomb a second time," he said.

Myanmar has been locked in civil war since the military staged a 2021 coup ousting Aung San Suu Kyi, and has been under martial rule since. The military, which is frequently accused of carrying out strikes on public buildings, has previously said it only strikes legitimate targets.

World.title: IJEBULAND: Inside story of the Awujale succession crisis
World.content:
•Amid claims of interference, factions emerge

By James Ogunnaike, Abeokuta

For Ijebuland, the wait for a new Awujale has become much more than a traditional succession exercise.

It has evolved into a complex contest involving custom, law, family interests, institutional authority and allegations of political influence.

More than a year after the death of Oba Sikiru Kayode Adetona, the late Awujale of Ijebuland, the kingdom is yet to produce a successor.

Instead, the process has been repeatedly suspended, challenged and reopened, with fresh disputes now emerging within the very ruling house expected to produce the next monarch.

The latest crisis in the Fusengbuwa Ruling House has added another layer to an already complicated succession saga.

At the centre of the latest dispute is the purported removal of three senior officials of the ruling house: Chairman, Otunba Abdulateef Owoyemi; Vice-Chairman, Prof. Fassy Yusuf; and Deputy Chairman, Prince Oladokun Ajidagba, over allegations of financial inducement, manipulation of documents and breach of due process.

But the trio has rejected the allegations and the purported removal, describing those behind the action as “usurpers and impostors.”

The competing claims have raised a fundamental question: Can Ijebuland choose a new Awujale without further damaging public confidence in the institution?

A throne of immense history

Oba Adetona died in July 2025 at the age of 91 after an extraordinary 65-year reign.

His reign transformed the Awujale stool into one of Nigeria’s most respected traditional institutions.

He was widely regarded as a monarch who combined tradition with modernity, while his outspoken interventions on national issues gave the throne an influence extending well beyond Ijebuland.

His death therefore created not merely a vacancy, but a profound institutional transition.

Under the Awujale Chieftaincy Declaration and the Ogun State Obas and Chiefs Law, succession rotates among the recognised ruling houses: Anikinaiya, Fusengbuwa, Fidipote and Gbelegbuwa.

Following the late monarch’s death, the turn fell to the Fusengbuwa Ruling House.

By December 2025, the Ijebu-Ode Local Government had formally invited the ruling house to commence the process of nominating candidates.

What followed was an unprecedented rush of interest.

No fewer than 95 aspirants; 94 princes and one princess reportedly emerged.

The sheer number reflected the prestige attached to the throne, but it also exposed the difficulty of administering a contest involving numerous branches, lineages and competing interpretations of eligibility.

Almost immediately, controversy followed.

Politics of succession

The succession process became increasingly contentious amid allegations that political interests were attempting to influence the outcome.

One of the most explosive allegations concerned a reported late-night meeting involving Governor Dapo Abiodun and kingmakers.

According to accounts attributed to people familiar with the meeting, the governor was alleged to have indicated support for Hon. Ademorin Kuye as his preferred candidate and urged the kingmakers to present him.

The allegation has been denied by the government, which has repeatedly insisted that it has no preferred candidate and is committed to due process.

Yet the reported meeting became a defining moment in the controversy.

Sources claimed that the kingmakers resisted what they regarded as political interference as the Awujale stool could not be treated as a political appointment.

One statement attributed to the confrontation captured the intensity of the disagreement: “No Kuye, no Awujale.”

The kingmakers were also reported to have responded that they would rather have no Awujale than accept an imposed monarch.

Whether every detail of the reported exchange can ultimately be established is a matter for those directly involved.

KWAM 1’s dramatic intervention

The crisis was further complicated by the entry of popular Fuji musician, Alhaji Wasiu Ayinde Marshal, popularly known as KWAM 1 or K1 De Ultimate.

The musician declared interest in the throne, claiming eligibility through the Jadiara branch of the Fusengbuwa Ruling House.

His claim was immediately disputed by leaders of the Fusengbuwa family and the Jadiara Royal House, who denied that he possessed the required paternal lineage and reportedly maintained that he belonged to the Fidipote Ruling House.

Through his lawyer, Dr Wahab Shittu, SAN, Ayinde challenged aspects of the nomination process, alleging exclusion and the use of a “delegate system” that, he claimed, disenfranchised some members.

He also alleged that security operatives prevented him from attending a nomination meeting on January 12, 2026.

The dispute eventually reached the Ogun State High Court in Ijebu-Ode. His application was dismissed, after which Ayinde withdrew both the suit and his bid for the throne.

His departure, however, did not end the controversy.

Government suspension

With petitions, protests and competing allegations multiplying, Ogun State government intervened.

The Commissioner for Local Government and Chieftaincy Affairs, Hon. Ganiyu Hamzat, warned against misinformation and cautioned individuals against parading themselves as ‘Awujale-elect.’

“The process is governed strictly by customary law and extant statutes,” Hamzat said, insisting that the government would remain neutral while enforcing due process.

On January 20, 2026, the government suspended the selection process, citing petitions, security reports and heightened tension.

The decision was presented as a measure intended to preserve peace and protect the dignity of the institution.

Chief Sonny Kuku, Chairman of the Awujale Interregnum Council and head of the kingmakers, confirmed the suspension and said consultations were ongoing.

He disclosed that the kingmakers had begun scrutinising more than 1,200 documents submitted by aspirants.

“There will be no imposition,” Kuku said. “The responsibility is too sacred.”

The state later nullified the exercise, citing procedural lapses by the local government, and ordered the Fusengbuwa Ruling House to restart the process.

That decision generated another dispute, with the Fidipote Ruling House arguing that Fusengbuwa had forfeited its turn by failing to meet statutory timelines.

The government rejected the argument, maintaining that the process had not legally commenced.

New battle inside Fusengbuwa

The latest crisis has moved the succession battle from the wider arena into the heart of the Fusengbuwa family.

A nine-member Fact-Finding Committee, constituted in June 2026 and chaired by Prince Olusegun Olusoga, was tasked with examining petitions concerning the conduct of the ruling house’s leadership and the nomination process.

The committee, according to its secretary, Ridwan Oduneye, produced a 25-page report.

Only Owoyemi appeared before the committee, while Yusuf and Ajidagba reportedly declined its invitation.

Oduneye said the committee found “a manifest breakdown of unity, communication, and cohesion” among the three officials recognised as Olori-Ebis.

The committee also alleged irregularities in the compilation and submission of candidates.

It faulted the leadership for allegedly failing to classify candidates according to categories provided in the Awujale Declaration, including male-line and female-line candidates and those born through Awujale Folagbade before he ascended the throne.

Oduneye described the alleged failure as “deliberate dereliction of sacred duty.”

The committee recommended that the three officials step aside.

At a general meeting of the ruling house on August 9, the recommendation was reportedly adopted by the faction that convened the meeting.

Speaking after the meeting, Adeyemi said the decision was unanimous.

Oduneye also alleged financial inducement, support for preferred candidates and manipulation of documents.

But these are allegations contained in a committee report, not judicial findings of criminal guilt.

That distinction is crucial.

Trio fight back

The affected officials have mounted a vigorous defence.

Yusuf, speaking on behalf of the trio, dismissed the allegations and rejected the purported removal.

He described those behind the action as “a bunch of rabble rousers and confusionists.”

He questioned the authority of the committee and the meeting that purportedly removed them, particularly because of an alleged interest in the Awujale contest by one of those involved.

“How could somebody under you set up a panel to probe you? Probe you for what? Who are they?” Yusuf asked.

He denied any role in compiling the candidate list and threatened legal action over alleged defamation.

Owoyemi was equally dismissive

“Their allegations are baseless, unfounded and should be ignored by members of the public,” he said, describing the group behind the purported removal as “a bunch of rebels.”

The dispute therefore presents Ijebuland with two irreconcilable narratives: one side says it is fighting to restore integrity and due process; the other insists that it is being targeted by an unauthorised faction attempting to seize control of the ruling house.

Grand Council backs trio

The dispute escalated when the Grand Council of the Fusengbuwa Ruling House passed a vote of confidence in Owoyemi, Ajidagba and Yusuf.

The council rejected their removal and described the opposing group as a “kangaroo committee.”

Owoyemi said the current leadership emerged after three factions within the family were reconciled through the intervention of Ogun State government.

According to him, the reconciled structure produced him as Chairman/Olori-Ebi, Ajidagba as Deputy Chairman and Yusuf as Vice-Chairman.

He said the opposing group had no authority to act for the family.

He alleged that the group was attempting to undermine Fusengbuwa’s claim to the Awujale throne.

The group also urged the governor to lift the suspension and allow the kingmakers to conclude their traditional responsibility.

Yusuf went further, arguing that the government had no legal authority to halt the process.

That position, however, remains contested by the state, which has relied on its statutory responsibilities under the Obas and Chiefs Law.

‘We only want due process’

Oduneye has rejected the charge that his group is attempting to overthrow the recognised leadership.

He said the objective was to “restore due process, unity and the integrity of the Fusegbuwa/Jadiara Ruling House.”

According to him, the August 9 meeting was attended by 115 members from different family lineages and resolved to remove the trio and appoint Prince Adeleke Adeyemi as interim secretary and authorised signatory pending the election of a new Olori-Ebi.

He welcomed the prospect of litigation.

“Litigation is a civil way of seeking redress. The court will be the best place to establish who has betrayed the House and who is pursuing personal interest at the expense of the collective,” Oduneye said.

He also denied having a personal interest in the succession contest, pointing to his family’s historical connection with the ruling house.

Kingmakers draw line

While the Fusengbuwa dispute rages, another disagreement emerged among the kingmakers.

The Awujale Afobaje Council, led by Chief Sonny Kuku, rejected a letter reportedly sent to Governor Abiodun by the Olisa of Ijebu-Ode, Chief Rasheed Adeoye Adesanya.

The Afobajes accused Adesanya of falsely presenting himself as chairman of the council and objected to his use of the appellation “Alaiyeluwa”, a title ordinarily associated with a reigning monarch.

According to the council, the law does not expressly designate a chairman, but at its inaugural meeting on December 2, 2025, Adesanya himself allegedly nominated Kuku as chairman, with the nomination unanimously supported.

The council said it subsequently held four meetings — on December 2, January 13, January 19 and January 20 — before halting its deliberations following the government’s suspension.

“We therefore urge all sons and daughters of Ijebu Ode, as well as residents of our ancient kingdom, to remain calm, peaceful, and law-abiding while awaiting the directive of the Ogun State government,” the statement said.

The council’s position is significant because the kingmakers occupy a central role in the traditional selection of the Awujale.

Their insistence on due process underscores the wider concern that competing claims of authority could further complicate the succession.

Question of public trust

At this stage, the biggest casualty of the prolonged dispute may be public confidence.

A traditional institution derives its authority not only from law or custom, but also from the acceptance of the people.

The Awujale stool has survived for generations because successive monarchs have been regarded as custodians of a collective heritage.

If the process of choosing the next occupant becomes synonymous with factional warfare, allegations of inducement, political pressure and competing claims of authority, the institution itself risks being diminished.

There is a strong argument, therefore, for separating allegations from established facts.

Claims of bribery or manipulation should not be treated as convictions. They should be independently investigated where appropriate. Those accused must be allowed to defend themselves, while anyone found to have compromised the process should face the consequences prescribed by law.

Equally, allegations of political interference should be tested against evidence rather than rumour.

What Ijebuland needs now is not another round of accusations, but an authoritative process capable of answering the outstanding questions.

Who is entitled to nominate? Who has authority to screen candidates?

What exactly constitutes eligibility under the Awujale Declaration? What role should government play?

What are the limits of the Afobajes’ powers? And, perhaps most importantly, what safeguards exist to prevent anyone with a personal interest in the outcome from controlling the process? These questions must be answered transparently.

Tradition must survive the test of modern governance

The Awujale institution is ancient, but the society around it is not.

Ijebuland today includes professionals, academics, business leaders, politicians, traditionalists and a large diaspora. Its people increasingly expect institutions, traditional and governmental to demonstrate transparency and accountability. That does not mean abandoning custom.

On the contrary, clear adherence to established custom may be the best defence against manipulation.

The strength of the Ijebu political and cultural system has historically rested on institutions such as the Osugbo, the ruling houses and the network of chiefs and community authorities. Those institutions can only retain their authority if their decisions are perceived as legitimate.

The lesson from the present crisis is therefore broader than the identity of the next Awujale. It is about whether tradition can be preserved while embracing procedures that withstand public scrutiny.

Danger of rushing the throne

There will inevitably be pressure to end the interregnum. But speed should not become the overriding objective. A monarch whose selection is challenged from the outset could spend the early years of his reign defending his legitimacy rather than uniting the kingdom.

By contrast, a painstaking process that addresses grievances, verifies documents, clarifies eligibility and resolves internal disputes may take longer, but could produce a stronger outcome.

The next Awujale must inherit not only the palace, but also the confidence of Ijebuland. That confidence cannot be manufactured by government proclamation, family declaration or media campaign.

It must emerge from a process that the major stakeholders the ruling houses, Afobajes, government and the wider Ijebu public regard as fair.

World.title: ABUJA SUBMERGED:‘We have not seen anything like this before’
World.content:
… One night, rain erases line between Asokoro and FCT suburbs, Maitama bleeds

By John Alechenu, ABUJA

The rain started in trickles, small drops at a time. Abuja, Nigeria’s capital city, is not immune to rainfall.

But by 10pm last Tuesday, it was no longer raindrops. It was a flood — the first of its kind in recent history. By the time the rains eased, it had caused serious upset in the city’s prime towns-Asokoro, Maitama, Guzape, Lokogoma, Garki and Wuse.

The tears arising from the flooding are still reverberating in the city and environs.

Nobody ever saw it coming, but it did with audacity; and atrocities followed.

Mallam Umar Abdullahi, who occupies a security house in one of the posh buildings in Asokoro, first heard the sound of rain on his roof.

He dismissed it and went about his routine.

But he was forced to leave his bed when he heard his daughter screaming, “Mummy, water is coming in.”

He got up and switched on his torchlight to see what was amiss.

By the time he reached the door, water had overtaken the entire compound and was already pushing in under the door.

Four streets away, a government official’s SUV was stuck halfway up the road.

The driver had thought it was a shallow puddle. It wasn’t.

In Maitama, Kuzape and Guzape, the story was no different.

Houses had been sunk, many gates removed and fences to mighty buildings removed with ease by the rampaging floods that rose from the rainfall.

“This is the first time since I came to Abuja over a decade ago that I’m experiencing this,” Nasir Tanko said.

That Tuesday night, Abuja’s flood story changed.

It stopped being about Kubwa, Lokogoma and Galadima.

The water came for the hills.

It came for Asokoro, Maitama and Guzape and Katampe.

‘We have never seen this before’

Mr. Emmanuel Okoro has lived on the same Asokoro Street since 2008. He retired from the civil service. He keeps a clean compound and pays his bills.

“14 years,” he said on Wednesday morning, pointing at a brown line on his wall, “water has never come this high.”

By 12:30am, the water was in his boys’ quarters.

He and his wife spent the night moving things to the top of wardrobes. His rug from Dubai is ruined.

The bookshelf in his study tilted and fell.

“I kept thinking this is Asokoro. This doesn’t happen here,” he said. “But water doesn’t know Asokoro from anywhere else.”

Across the road, an embassy car was being towed out. Water was still dripping from the exhaust. The driver, a young man in his 30s, sat on the curb looking tired.

“Oga said I should try to pass. Now look.”

In Maitama, the damage was not just to properties alone. It disrupted the pride of Maitama, where the high and the influential in Nigeria, reside with lush.

Zainab, 34, who works in a bank in the CBD, got home at 8pm. By 11pm she was moving her mother and the children upstairs. Her husband was out of town.

“I looked down and saw the kitchen under water. The fridge had fallen. The smell the next day… mud, diesel, sewage. You can’t wash that out in one day.”

Her househelp, Amina, also slept upstairs with the rest of the family. “Her room was gone: Mattress, clothes, everything. She was crying. She said, ‘Aunty, my salary is in that bag.’”

Guzape takes the worst hit

Guzape is where Abuja is building mansions: Big gates, hillside views, duplexes that cost hundreds of millions of naira. Call it the FCT’s version of Lekki in Lagos and you may not be wrong. The area was washed up and its residents cannot still understand what hit them.

For the past five years, the place has been one big construction site. On Tuesday, all that construction collided with water.

“Water was coming from three places,” Tunde said. He’s a site engineer. “From the hill behind us, from the road they are still doing, and from the next estate. We did sandbags. The water just pushed them.”

He lost bags of cement, rods and tiles worth over N2 million. His client called him Wednesday morning. “Tunde, is this what we paid for?”

“What do I say?” Tunde asked. “That the hill decided to cry?”

Down the road, a newly completed duplex had its fence crushed by the water. The owner, a businessman based in Lagos, flew in on Thursday. He stood in his compound and didn’t say anything for a long time.

Morning after: Mud and questions

By Wednesday, the sun was out. It felt like a mockery. Men were outside with brooms and wheelbarrows. FEMA trucks were moving around. Some roads were still closed. The road linking part of Guzape to the expressway was cut off.

In a WhatsApp group for one Asokoro Street, someone posted a video of a man “kayaking” with a plastic chair. People laughed. Then someone posted a photo of a collapsed wall. The chat went quiet.

Mrs. Aisha Dogo sells provisions in Maitama. She lost a deep freezer and bags of rice.

“We pay ground rent. We pay tax. The drainage here has not been cleared in years. Now look,” Mrs. Dogo lamented.

The anger was the same everywhere. “We were told these areas have a master plan,” said a diplomat whose two official cars were submerged in Asokoro.

He didn’t want his name in print. “So where did the water go?”

As residents and businesses tried to assess the damage, news began to make the rounds that demolition squads were about to be unleashed.

Many agree the flood was not a natural disaster. It was the product of years of abuse of the Abuja master plan. Structures were built on waterways. Drainages were sand-filled and allotted to powerful individuals and developers. Green areas were destroyed and, in their places, new high-rise buildings for private and commercial use, sprang up.

What went wrong

Engineers and planners say it wasn’t just one thing.

First, the rain. NiMet data showed over 90mm fell in less than four hours that night.

That’s the kind of downpour Abuja gets once in several years.

Second, the drains. Most of the drainage in the city centre is outdated and silted.

It was built for a smaller Abuja, with more trees and fewer houses. Over the years, silt and refuse have reduced their capacity.

Third, Guzape. The hills have been cut and built on.

Natural water paths are now roads and houses. When rain falls on a hill with concrete, it runs faster.

A contractor working in Guzape put it simply: “When you build on a water path, water will find another path. Sometimes that path is through your parlour.”

He didn’t want his name published. “We keep telling clients, leave setbacks. Leave drainage. But everybody wants to use the whole land.”

An FCDA official, who also asked not to be named, said the authority had started desilting some channels last month.

“But you can’t clear 30 years of blockage in one month. And people still dump refuse in drains.”

The small stories

The big damage makes the news. The small damage is what people remember.

A five-year-old girl in Maitama thought the flood was fun until she saw her toys floating.

Her mother had to fish a teddy bear out of the gutter.

Chinedu manages a restaurant on a Maitama corner.

He threw away food worth N800, 000. “Three days closed. Staff at home. Landlord is still asking for rent. I don’t know what to do”, he told Sunday Vanguard.

For domestic staff, it was worse. Many sleep in boys’ quarters that are usually the lowest part of a compound.

“My gateman’s room was full,” Mr. Okoro said. “We had to bring him to sleep in our store. He lost everything.”

In Guzape, labourers lost a week’s wages because the site was underwater. “No work, no pay,” one of them said as he carried cement bags to dry them.

How did we get here?

Former FCT Council Chairman of the Nigeria Union of Journalists, Emmanuel Ogbeche, said the flood was long in coming.

“For a long time, some of us have voiced our concerns over the indiscretion of the FCT Minister in allocating green areas, gardens and open spaces,” he said.

“If anyone cares to remember, I raised alarm over the narrowing of the canal at Gudu/Apo just opposite Bakangizo Supermarket. The flash flood that overwhelmed the garden there can’t be separated from the building of the estate ongoing there.

“In Maitama, most open spaces have been cannibalised by the government that is supposed to protect and defend its master plan at all costs.

“Would areas he allocated and took over, like those meant for public hospitals in Guzape and Wuye, be revoked to their original intent?

“Would the vexatious logging of wood in the city be halted? Abuja can’t thrive as a city of concrete and steel. Let the trees breathe.”

Government response

By Tuesday afternoon, officials from FEMA and FCDA were going around with trucks and pumping machines.

The Director of FEMA, in a short briefing, said the agency was “assessing the extent of damage” and would “engage relevant departments to address drainage issues.” He also appealed to residents to stop dumping refuse.

The Minister of the FCT, Nyesom Wike, was on ground to assess the damage as soon as the rains stopped. He acknowledged the abuse of water channels by individuals and groups and promised action.

Within hours, he ordered demolitions. Cranes, bulldozers, tippers and armed security forces stormed Mississippi Street and surrounding areas in Maitama and began pulling down homes, fences and businesses. There was no room to plead for mercy.

Business owners in parts of Maitama Extension and around the old WAEC building were caught off guard.

Owner of popular business venture Xpressor, Mustapha Onimisi, told reporters: “We were told yesterday by a Director in FCDA that they would mark our property and give us two weeks to move valuables.

“But to our shock, we woke up this morning and heard Wike was here himself and ordered the demolitions. It is sad. This should have been better handled.”

Other residents say they need more than statements. “We need to see action,” said a residents’ association chairman in Asokoro.

“Let them come and open the drains. Let them tell us if we need to do anything differently.”

‘Tell us the truth’

By Wednesday, people were sweeping. But they were also asking questions.

“Government should tell us the truth,” Mr. Okoro said. “If this place can flood again, let us know. We can’t be living in fear every time it rains.”

Mrs. Dogo was more direct. “We don’t dump in the drain. But when rain falls like that for four hours, where should it go? We need bigger drains. We need maintenance every year, not once in five years.”

In Guzape, estate developers held a meeting on Thursday. The agenda: Drainage and retention basins. “People are scared,” said one developer. “They’re asking if their investment is safe. We have to answer them.”

A new fear

The biggest change is in people’s heads. Before, when it rained, people in Asokoro worried about traffic. Now they check weather apps.

On Wednesday night, the message in estate groups was the same: “Clouds are gathering. Park on high ground. Charge your phone. Move documents upstairs.”

Kids have found a new game. They’re racing paper boats in the gutters. Parents are shouting.

Tunde is back on site, trying to salvage what’s left: “This is Nigeria. You build, rain falls, you build again. But I didn’t expect to be rebuilding in Guzape.”

Zainab bought rubber boots on Wednesday. “For next time,” she said. “Because there will be a next time.”

The line has blurred

For years, Abuja people had a way of talking about flooding. “That one is for Kubwa people.” “That one is for Lokogoma.”

But on Tuesday night, the flood hit the high and the mighty in Asokoro and erased their pride and safety. For a few hours, it didn’t matter if one was a minister or a trader. Everyone in Asokoro, Maitama or Guzape were knee-deep in the same water.

It also raised a bigger question about Abuja’s growth. The city was planned for a little over three million people. It now has close to 10 million. The infrastructure is stretched.

“You can’t have a capital city where the centre floods and we call it normal,” said an urban planner. “We need to retrofit the old drainage. And we need to enforce planning rules in new areas like Guzape.”

Mrs. Yusuf is drying her books in the sun. Some will survive. Some won’t.

“I love this house,” she said. “But next time they say ‘heavy rain’, I’m sleeping upstairs with my documents in a Ghana-must-go bag.”

The hills are still standing. The houses are still standing. But after Tuesday night, no one in Abuja’s power corridor is taking the rain for granted again.

And everyone is watching the sky.

Wike is really upset with the flooding of the city and the destruction it caused. He does not want a repeat of the flooding anymore.

First, he has ordered the demolition of any structure standing on a water channel irrespective of the owner.

The FCT Minister has also banned the conversion of green spaces, parks and gardens into commercial car dealership lots across Abuja.

The directive is part of measures by the FCT Administration to curb worsening flood incidents across the capital city, where the loss of designated absorption zones and recreational spaces has disrupted urban drainage systems.

Senior Special Assistant on Public Communications and Social Media to the FCT Minister, Lere Olayinka, disclosed this in a statement Wednesday in Abuja.

To ensure total compliance, the FCT Administration has established a dedicated Task Force tasked with monitoring affected areas and enforcing the immediate clearance of illegal car lots.

In addition to the operational ban, the Minister has initiated an administrative probe into officials suspected of issuing illegal approvals for the commercial use of these protected areas.

How far these measures would be implemented and sustained, remains to be seen as terrified residents continue to watch the sky of Abuja.

World.title: It was a mistake that Tinubu did not attend Peace Accord signing—Adebayo, SDP presidential candidate
World.content:
By Olalekan Bilesanmi

The 2027 presidential candidate of the Social Democratic Party (SDP), Adewole Adebayo, says genuine peace in Nigeria’s electoral process can only be achieved when there is justice, transparency and strict adherence to the law. According to Adebayo, who spoke in an interview following the signing of the 2027 Electoral Peace Accord, political parties and candidates should not regard the agreement as a favour to the country, but as a commitment to conduct themselves in accordance with the law. He criticises President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for failing to personally attend the peace accord ceremony, describing the president’s absence as a wrong signal to Nigerians and law enforcement agencies. Adebayo also calls for greater independence for the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), insisting that the police, Department of State Services (DSS), civil defence and military should remain politically neutral during elections. Below are excerpts from the interview:

You signed the peace accord. What exactly did you commit to?

Basically, what I committed to is what the law says: elections must be based on issues. We have always campaigned on issues. We do not attack personalities, and we do not campaign against identities. We do not use identity to campaign. There is no issue of religion, ethnicity and all of that. We totally avoid hate speech, and we don’t use bad language. We don’t use fake news. We don’t use false propaganda, and we try as much as possible to comply with the Electoral Act in terms of how to conduct rallies. We totally avoid violence. We don’t use thugs. We don’t pay thugs. We don’t buy votes, and we don’t sell votes. We don’t do money politics. We respect the office that we are running for, and we conduct ourselves as if we have already taken the oath of office for that position.

That is what I signed, and that is what I am committed to. I signed not only with my hand; I signed with my heart, and I intend to live up to it.

I also commend the Peace Committee for taking this matter seriously, even though some people in the political space, especially those in government, take it as a joke and are not serious about it. However, the Peace Committee is taking it seriously. The chairman and members of the committee have shown Nigerians that it is possible to pursue a national objective without being in government and to do so consistently over the years in search of peace.

The reason why we have not managed to have peace so far is that peace is impossible without justice.

Electoral justice will bring peace automatically in a system where every player in the electoral process follows the law; where the government of the day does not put its thumb on the scale; where INEC is truly independent and follows the mandate given to it to conduct free, fair and credible elections; and where voters vote according to their conscience and consciousness.

Whether they vote for the right person or not, let them vote freely, without inducement and without harassment. Let the result be the mathematical and arithmetical exactitude of what the voters actually voted. That will automatically bring peace. You don’t even need a Peace Committee searching for peace that is not missing, because the tool for getting peace is justice. When you do electoral justice, peace will come automatically.

So, you are saying that there is no peace without justice. Are you saying that you do not trust the electoral system under which you are asking people to vote?

What I am saying is that the electoral system needs a lot of improvement. When I become president, I will not short-circuit INEC as chairman. I will not control its money.

That’s not your forte. The law says that if you become president, you determine that.

I will change the law because laws are made by people. Those laws do not write themselves.

In fact, when President Umaru Musa Yar’Adua came into office, one of the things he agreed with us on was to set up a panel to try to change that system.

So, depending on the circumstances at that time, we will work to make INEC independent. Let law enforcement agencies—the police, DSS, civil defence and all branches of the military—be totally agnostic to politics. Let them not influence politics. Let them not take political instructions.

Let their presence during elections not even be a subject for discussion. Let elections be free, fair and civilised. With that, I can guarantee you that, as president, the Peace Committee will be idle during my time, because the person who has the greatest possibility of establishing peace in the land is the president of the country or the governor of a state.

If you look at recent elections, peace accords were signed. Yet, if you look at some of those governors who left their states and were seen making trouble here and there, including the Minister of the FCT, who said, “If I was there, APC would not have lost,” those are the kinds of things that threaten peace.

Is it a crime for you to go and support your party member? Don’t you go around to support candidates running for election under your platform?

There are two things we need to consider. One, when you go to campaign, you don’t go as a lawless wanderer. You go peacefully like any other person. You make speeches that are consistent with the peace and good governance of the place, and you do not come and display massive state power. You go in a civilised way. If you have friends in a state, you use your friendship and goodwill. You go and campaign and say, “Vote for my party,” but not through this organised invasion that they organise. It is not proper. Those are the things which, if you do them, will make a difference.

I want us to understand that, in signing the peace accord, we are not doing the country a favour. We are committing ourselves to what we ordinarily should do. When I read through it, I didn’t see anything that I wasn’t already doing included there.

I think it is in the Bible that they say it is only the sick who needs the physician, and the people who needed the physician did not come.

President Tinubu, who is the number-one promoter of election violence and the promoter of all the confusion, refused to come. Maybe he doesn’t want to be committed to it. Maybe he feels that—

He sent a representative, the Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF).

Oh, please! This is an insult to the process. The SGF is not involved in the election. You have your Vice President, who could have come. I don’t see any reason why President Tinubu, who works and lives in Abuja and who has the influence to determine when the event would be held, and who gave an indication that he would come, failed to attend. I think President Tinubu has been missing in action for some time. I don’t know if you, as reporters, have noticed.

I don’t know if he is a ghost worker or whatever he is, because a president cannot be so invisible like that.

But we see him at meetings receiving guests in the Presidential Villa.

Oh, okay. Today?

We understand that he has had a closed-door meeting with the Senate President.

Closing his door is not doing our work. I’m talking about the president showing up in places where presidents are supposed to show up.

Do you count his absence as an insult, or how do you interpret it? If you were President Bola Tinubu and you had other presidential candidates…

I should be president myself. I can’t be President Bola Tinubu. That’s not a good example to use. What I can say is that there isn’t anything—I can’t say it is an insult because the behaviour of President Tinubu generally is an insult.

His regular behaviour is an insult to the country: the way he speaks, the way he conducts his affairs and the way he does not obey the law. His standard behaviour as president is already an automatic insult to the country, and he thinks he can do things anyhow.

I want to be respectful, but you cannot be running presidential lawlessness. A system where the president has no code of conduct—I don’t know whether he has no advisers. The president is the tone-setter for the country. So, to disregard things and disparage things—the president wanted to ridicule the process by his absence and by the nonchalance with which he handled it, and by the level of deputation that he made.

If you are signing a contract, you cannot designate somebody who has no capacity to sign the contract. If it was a contract, which it is, it would not be valid.

But in law, surrogation is allowed.

Surrogation is allowed where the law establishing that power allows surrogation.

In fact, in law, you cannot delegate certain things. You cannot delegate—What about Atiku?

You are talking only about Tinubu. Atiku and the ADC were also absent.

You know, Atiku is a person seeking the presidency, not the president. The president has a duty to the country.

I have a duty to the country, but my duty is less than that of the president. When I become president, you will see my behaviour.

Prince Adewole Adebayo is one of those who signed the peace accord today. The peace-signing ceremony is an indication of the commitment of those participating in the 2027 general election to peaceful conduct ahead of the elections. Campaigns will resume tomorrow. What do you see ahead of this election? INEC says it is committed, is not biased, does not belong to any political party and will conduct free, fair and credible elections. Do you believe INEC?

I say Amen. It’s a prayer, and it is something we need to make happen. It is not that INEC can make it happen on its own. It is a desire that I can never go against. But there are steps we need to take. I don’t even know whether INEC has received all the money it needs to conduct the election, because President Tinubu and his government have managed to put INEC in a position where it cannot plan properly. They are holding its money. They are holding it to ransom. I think INEC doesn’t belong to the president. It doesn’t belong to any candidate. It doesn’t belong to any party. That is the law of the land. It is left for Nigerians to make sure that this election is one we take advantage of and that we do all we can to participate.

There are over 100 million voters. We should try to get at least 85 to 90 million people to come out and vote according to their conscience, without selling their votes. That is important.

As for the campaign, you will see that the SDP has brought its manifesto, focused on poverty and insecurity, and we will launch it very soon in Abuja. We are already going around the country, exchanging ideas with people, talking to sector leaders and talking to all shades of opinion in the country to develop everything contained in Chapter Two of our Constitution—the Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy. We want to see a country where no one is hungry, no one is homeless, no one is without medical care, no one who wants to work is without employment, and every child is guaranteed the maximum education necessary to develop his or her talent.

Those are the things the SDP will sell. We want to move Nigeria away from the poverty that has afflicted the country for decades, so that no Nigerian will say that poverty is their destiny for life under our government.

That is what we are focused on. But it is important that this election be conducted in an atmosphere that is free, fair, credible and peaceful.

President Tinubu’s failure to show up today is sending the signal that he is not committed to peace. He is sending the wrong signal to law enforcement agencies and to people who work for the government—that the president does not appear to be committed enough.

He needs to correct that by making a clear statement, explaining why he was absent and making sure that he commits himself publicly to peace.

Might it be a matter of what—and I’m just playing devil’s advocate here—what if he was held up by issues of state?

There is no issue of state greater than the president showing that democracy is important.

Even with national security? President Buhari said that issues of national security and democratic values sometimes need to be considered. You need the debate around national security, and when it comes to issues of democracy, you need to be able to…

There is no greater national security than the continuity of the state. The state has to assist, and a free, fair and credible election is important for establishing civil government.

What moral event of today can be considered equal to issues of national security?

It is the most important issue in the country because of the continuity of democracy. It is this process that made him president—the process of election. Four years ago, he was around, and now—

President Buhari was not even contesting. The most committed president so far since the process began has been President Goodluck Jonathan. It is good for you as a leader to signal that we are a civilised society and that we believe in the peace process. If we look at eminent Nigerians such as John Onaiyekan and other people who are in that Peace Committee, Professor Ameze Gubadia, General Martin Luther Agwai and others, these are eminent people in their respective careers who could have been president if they had run for election. So, it is important for the president to be serious and send that signal down because, as the leader of the country, if you say peace doesn’t matter, then you can be absent.

From what I understand, everything was done to accommodate the president, including the timing and date, and he gave his word that he was going to be there. It is something personal because he is the one elected; he is the one who will make the commitment. I have a feeling that, in addition to President Tinubu’s tardy way of behaving recently, where he doesn’t show up and just locks himself up somewhere nobody knows where he is, he has contempt for the peace process. He doesn’t want to sit down and commit himself to being peaceful.

Legally speaking, he is not bound by it. It is a moral issue, not a legal issue.

He is bound by it because he has a constitutional mandate to be a moral leader. When he took that oath of office on May 29, 2023, he swore to respect the Constitution of Nigeria. The Constitution of Nigeria says we should have free, fair and credible elections. The Electoral Act also has provisions which the president and his people violated in Osun. Do you know what it means for a country to be clapping and saying that we had a governorship election when there were 41 people or more in the mortuary? How do you do that? What kind of country allows a system where people lose their lives and limbs, where people are lynched in the afternoon?

A president who has seen that should use this opportunity to come forward and even make a comment, saying, “My government will investigate what happened in Osun. It will not happen again.” President Tinubu has proven that it is a moral failure, and a moral failure is not what the country needs to be.

World.title: 2027 campaigns: All eyes on Tinubu, Atiku, Obi amid anxiety over hate speech, personal attacks
World.content:
By Dapo Akinrefon & Gabriel Ewepu

As the campaigns for the 2027 general elections begin following the signing of the Peace Accord last week by presidential candidates, there are fears over the likelihood of the exercise snowballing into brinkmanship.

Specifically, there are concerns that the contest could descend into an increasingly bitter and divisive struggle, with hate speech, ethnic profiling, misinformation and political violence threatening to overshadow the issues that matter most to Nigerians.

The presidential and National Assembly campaigns officially commenced on Tuesday, August 19, 2026, and would run until January 15, 2027, exactly 24 hours before the presidential and National Assembly elections scheduled for January 16, 2027.

Also, the governorship and state House of Assembly campaigns would commence on September 9, 2026, and end on February 5, 2027, ahead of the elections scheduled for February 6, 2027.

Last week, some presidential candidates signed the National Peace Accord, thereby committing themselves to peaceful conduct and issue-based campaigns ahead of the elections.

The accord, facilitated by the National Peace Committee and supported by the Kukah Centre, is expected to serve as a framework for responsible political engagement as the parties and their candidates intensify mobilisation across the country.

Presidential candidates who signed the Peace Accord include Mr Peter Obi of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), Prince Adewole Adebayo of the Social Democratic Party (SDP) and Mr Omoyele Sowore of the African Action Congress (AAC).

President Bola Tinubu, who is the presidential candidate of the All Progressive Congress (APC) in the January 2027 election, was represented at the occasion by the Secretary to the Federal Government, Mr George Akume, while the candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Alhaji Atiku Abubakar, simply stayed away without offering explanation for his action.

Tinubu, Atiku and Obi are widely believed to be the main candidates in the presidential election.

Significantly, Atiku just recently dragged Tinubu to court over his qualifications for the election, alleging that, contrary to his claims in the forms submitted to the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), the president never participated in the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC).

The NDC candidate is also pursuing a case in the United States (U.S.) in which he is asking the FBI to release details of a drug case in which Tinubu forfeited some funds to the country’s government.

This appears to be a replay of the 2023 episode in which both candidates in then-presidential election resorted to personal attacks.

For Atiku and Obi, their supporters have resorted to a bitter struggle in support of their candidates.

Election cycles

Meanwhile, apprehension, according to findings by Sunday Vanguard, is rooted partly in the experience of previous election cycles, particularly the 2011, 2015 and 2023 presidential elections, when political rhetoric frequently took on ethnic, religious, violent and regional dimensions.

Nigerian election campaigns have also repeatedly been criticised for being driven more by personality attacks, ethnic and religious mobilisation, defections and political calculations than by sustained debates on competing policies and programmes.

For instance, last week’s governorship election in Osun State wasn’t an exception, as no fewer than 40 people were reportedly killed in the pre-election period.

This is why, in various conversations with Sunday Vanguard, key stakeholders in the electoral process, including Civil Society Organisations, CSOs, lawyers and regional groups, among others, cautioned political parties, candidates and their supporters against hate speech, ethnic profiling and violence, urging them to make the 2027 contest a battle of ideas focused on the economy, security, unemployment, education, healthcare and other issues affecting Nigerians.

Social media may be weaponised — Odumakin

Speaking on the matter, President, Centre for Change, Dr Joe Okei Odumakin, said though she remains worried about hate speech, ethnic and religious profiling, her greatest fears are the weaponisation of social media.

She said: “My greatest concern ahead of the 2027 general elections is the possibility of political competition degenerating into hate speech, ethnic and religious profiling, misinformation, character assassination and violence.

“Elections should be a contest of ideas, policies, competence and character, not a war between ethnic or religious groups.

“We must reject narratives portraying any ethnic group or region as an enemy simply because of its political preference.”

She, however, said Nigerians should be allowed to choose their leaders without intimidation or discrimination.

Odumakin said: “Nigeria belongs to all of us, and every citizen must be free to support any candidate or political party without intimidation or discrimination.

“I am particularly worried about the weaponisation of social media, where false information, manipulated videos and inflammatory statements can spread within minutes and create tension in communities.

“Political leaders, their supporters, influencers and the media must, therefore, exercise responsibility. “Candidates should challenge the records and policies of their opponents rather than resort to mudslinging and unsubstantiated allegations.

“Security agencies and relevant institutions must also respond promptly to credible threats and ensure that political actors do not turn their supporters into instruments of violence.

“My message is simple: Campaign vigorously, but campaign responsibly. “Attack policies, not ethnicities, expose wrongdoing, but do not manufacture allegations, mobilise supporters, but never mobilise them for violence.

“Nigerians must remember that political opponents are not enemies.

“After the election, we will still remain neighbours, colleagues, friends and fellow citizens.

“The 2027 elections should therefore be a contest of ideas and leadership, not hatred, ethnicity or violence.
