World.title: ‘Unbelievable’: Hanson intervenes after One Nation MP claims migration target ‘not too different’ from Labor’s
World.content:
PoliticsFederalImmigration ‘Unbelievable’: Hanson intervenes after One Nation MP claims migration target ‘not too different’ from Labor’s Matthew Knott Updated August 23, 2026 — 2:51pm ,first published 10:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One Nation has been plunged into disarray over immigration policy, with leader Pauline Hanson forced to intervene and shoot down MP David Farley’s stunning concession that the party’s headline migration figure would be scarcely different to the Albanese government’s. Farley sought to redefine the meaning of net overseas migration (NOM) in an interview on Sunday, arguing there was a “true form” of the figure that differs to the way it has long been officially calculated. One Nation MP David Farley has sought to clarify the party’s migration targets. Janie Barrett “Well, the raw number is not too different [to the government’s], but the reality is, where do we need them?” Farley told the ABC’s Insiders on Sunday. “We don’t need them in the great urban metroplex. We need them out to be productive, working in agriculture, engineering, mining, etc.”



Editor's pick Immigration One Nation flip-flops on migration policy, announces tobacco excise cut He continued: “I think the big difference is we’re focusing on what are the skills we need as a nation, where do we need these migrants to be? But the raw number is not too different.” Labor and the Coalition leapt upon Farely’s comments to argue that One Nation was divided and lacking clarity on a crucial policy for the party, which has put slashing migration at the centre of its pitch to voters. Amid confusion over its migration policy, One Nation last week clarified that its plan to cap visas was based on a net overseas migration target of 130,000 a year. In his Insiders interview, Farley said this figure did not include a raft of key migrant categories and that these workers would add at least 100,000 people to the target.



“Well, what we’re doing is we’re focusing on the NOM in its true form, he said. “Now, on top of the NOM, of course, we’ve got all the other programs that we run, the PALM program, which is important to my electorate of Farrer, the skilled registered aged care nurses etc are all very important,” he said. The Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme includes around 40,000 workers a year, he said, while aged care nurses would add around another 70,000 – plus more in the engineering and mechanical fields. Migrants are included in the official NOM figure if they stay in the country for a total of 12 months within a 16-month window regardless of their visa category. Farley, elected in a byelection in May, said that “at a minimum” there would be 100,000 extra migrants on top of One Nation’s130,000 target “but the 130,000 is what we call the ‘true NOM’” .



The federal government’s net overseas migration target is 245,000 for 2026-27 and 225,000 for each of the following two years, around the same as Farely’s total estimate of around 230,000. Hanson rejected Farley’s assertion that the party’s migration target was similar to Labor’s in a lengthy social media post on Sunday afternoon, insisting: “One Nation’s policy is to cut net overseas migration to 130,000. “The cuts will come from fewer international students and dependants, a dramatic reduction in temporary graduate visas and their dependants, and a much more targeted skilled migration program focused on the skills Australia genuinely needs ... One Nation’s target is less than half Labor’s current level.” Coalition Home Affairs spokesman Jonno Duniam accused One Nation of making policy on the run on a totemic issue for the party. “One Nation’s migration policy seems to change every time one of its MPs gets in front of a microphone,” Duniam said.



“It is unbelievable that, after years of One Nation campaigning on immigration, Australians still can’t get a straight answer about what their migration policy actually is.” Duniam said Farely had conceded that “One Nation’s headline migration figure certainly bares little resemblance to the actual number of people they would allow into Australia”. Energy Minister Chris Bowen accused Farely of being at odds with Hanson, who recently declared she doesn’t care if migration cuts affect Australian businesses. He said Farely appeared to be “on board” with the government’s efforts to reduce migration while not harming businesses that rely on foreign labor. Bowen said that “the numbers he was talking about are very similar to the numbers the government’s been working towards”.



“I’m not sure what One Nation is saying about immigration because it appears to me, based on what Mr Farley said, that One Nation now agrees with the approach of the government,” he said. Liberal housing spokesman Andrew Bragg has nominated under 180,000 as the size of net overseas migration under a Coalition government. During this year’s byelection, Farley broke with party policy during a candidate forum by suggesting it was “probably not” an issue if Australia’s net migration reached 306,000. “If we’re successful in One Nation’s water policies, we’re going to need more labour, and we’re going to need more labour quickly, skilled labour,” he said. World.title: Trump’s desperate move to mess with markets is destined to fail
World.content:
BusinessThe economyTrump's America Opinion Trump’s desperate move to mess with markets is destined to fail

Jonathan Levin August 23, 2026 — 2:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

With the midterm elections less than three months away, President Donald Trump’s Treasury Department is starting to look desperate about the soaring cost to borrow. The Treasury said it would increase its buybacks of longer-term government bonds “by at least double”, an amount that analysts figure would bring purchases to $US32 billion ($45 billion) per quarter. Make no mistake about the motivations: 30-year bond yields this week hit their highest since 2007, pushing borrowing costs higher for the government, businesses and consumers. US President Donald Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. Bessent’s Treasury has so far failed in its stated goal to get longer-term borrowing costs lower. Bloomberg Key mortgage rates are back up to around 7 per cent, a fresh blow to voters that were promised easier financing conditions under this government and ended up getting more of the same. US public debt surpassed $US40 trillion for the first time, and has now surged by a third in less than five years, as US lawmakers continue to shrug off calls to contend with historically wide fiscal deficits. In many ways, hedge fund manager turned Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is doing his best impression of King Canute, whose attempt to command the incoming tide to stop inevitably failed.



The Treasury described the buybacks, planned to start September 9, as a form of “liquidity support” — which is what they were intended to be when the program was created in 2024. In this case, “liquidity support” is a clever euphemism for “please bring yields down!” Related Article Opinion

Japan Why fears of a Japanese implosion have the world on edge Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist It’s an inappropriate co-opting of a program that was created to improve market functioning and the government’s cash management, and, as explicitly described by the previous administration, was “not intended to ameliorate periods of acute market stress” — like now. But that’s the way the market sees it, driving yields on 30-year Treasuries lower by as much as 0.10 percentage point on the news. The market’s reaction isn’t surprising. This is only the latest ill-conceived attempt at influencing market forces by the Bessent treasury, which has failed in its stated goal to get longer-term borrowing costs lower. In the administration’s 19 months in office, he has adjusted capital requirements to encourage banks to hold more bonds; supported the GENIUS Act which established a framework for stablecoins to invest in US government securities; and authorised US support for yen intervention, a move that looked custom-designed to dissuade a major foreign holder of Treasury bonds from dumping them to buy its own currency. Don’t expect today’s bond market move to last very long. For those keeping score, none of the above moves have made much of an enduring difference. The effects of the yen intervention in late July started fading almost immediately. And even though the buybacks will double from $US16 billion on a quarterly basis, it’s still minuscule given both the size of the $US31.5 trillion Treasury market and the massive global forces keeping longer-term Treasury yields from falling.



For one, inflation is making a comeback in Japan after a quarter of a century of quiescence. Japanese 10-year government yields, which compete for the money of foreign investors with Treasuries, are now roughly at their highest in 30 years. With the Bank of Japan expected to resume lifting benchmark interest rates by October, the move higher in yields may be just getting started. In the interconnected global financial system, that’s an earthquake that is being felt in all bond markets – and certainly not one the US can counteract with $US32 billion of buybacks per quarter. Also working against Bessent’s scheming is the fact that longer-term investment-grade corporate borrowing has surged to support the buildout of artificial intelligence. Earlier this month, Alphabet sold $US25 billion of bonds in dollars with maturities of up to 40 years. Amazon and SpaceX have likewise been among recent issuers of longer-dated bonds, with bond investors starting to show signs of indigestion. High interest rates are weighing on American consumers. Bloomberg Where the administration actually has a chance to meaningfully and responsibly impact borrowing costs, it has mostly declined to do so. Thanks to the extension of tax cuts to the wealthy last year, the US continues to post record budget deficits, with the shortfall on pace to grow by 5 per cent from 2025. Persistently warm inflation, fanned by Trump’s tariffs and the oil shock from his war with Iran, has also done its part to keep borrowing costs higher. (And while Trump didn’t start the inflation, he’s consistently missed the opportunity to end it.)



One generous interpretation of these developments is that Bessent is effectively making a market-timing bet. By combining buybacks of longer-term bonds with issuance that’s front-loaded in shorter-term securities such as Treasury bills, Bessent is wagering that yields will be lower in the months or years ahead – and that inflation, the AI borrowing glut and the Japanese market moves are transitory. If he is right, Bessent would be vindicated, but it’s the longest of long-shot bets. Related Article US politics Trump’s 2024 grocery photo op now haunts Republicans in the midterms Treasury shouldn’t be in the business of using taxpayer money to time markets like a hedge fund. Don’t forget that Bessent attacked his predecessor, Janet Yellen, for ostensibly similar tactics. If he’s wrong, which is highly likely, this will all go down as a brash attempt to paper over the reality of global bond markets: yields are going to stay relatively high for a considerable time, and the Trump administration will inevitably disappoint the voters that it courted with the promised lower borrowing costs. Carlton captain Patrick Cripps has guided his team into the wildcard finals. Getty Images

But the AFL will wait to officially announce which match will be played in each timeslot until after Hawthorn’s match against West Coast, which could still change the make-up of the top six.

That is relevant to the wildcard fixture because the team that finishes fifth will play the ladder’s lowest advancing team, while sixth will play the higher-ranked team of the winners.

World.title: ACT Party takes aim at 'activist judges', Treaty of Waitangi clauses
World.content:
The ACT Party has released a policy designed to protect core democratic values and property rights, reign in "activist judges" and stop Parliament creating "divisive" Treaty of Waitangi clauses.

"Today's policy is about ensuring New Zealanders can move forward under one law for all with one future together," party leader David Seymour said.

"ACT will add three principles to the Constitution Act, affirming the basic values that Parliament is sovereign, the rule of law is fundamental and all New Zealanders are equal before the law."

Key to the policy is restraining courts from considering Māori tikanga (custom) in decisions.

"Recent Supreme Court decisions have pushed the line further than Parliament ever legislated," Seymour said.

"Parliament has pushed back in some instances, such as Smith v Fonterra and the Marine and Coastal Area cases, but others, such as Ellis, where the Supreme Court widely expanded the use of tikanga in the law, have not been responded to.

"Parliament is elected, judges are not. We cannot allow tikanga to become a separate source of law applying to broad areas of unrelated law without Parliament ever deciding that it should.

"ACT will make clear that tikanga cannot be used to influence court decisions, except where Parliament has expressly allowed for it."

The party would also amend the Legislation Act 2019 to ensure statutes are enacted in the context of the time they were passed. Judges could resolve ambiguity, but not override statutory language.

"Courts are often responding to unclear legislation or Parliament's silence, when they make decisions that substantially change how the law is understood.

"ACT will stop governments writing vague treaty clauses into law that create uncertainty, and leave courts and officials to decide what they mean through divisive interpretations."

Any bill referring to the Waitangi Treaty would require cabinet to agree which interests were engaged, who they apply to and what obligations they created, restoring "clear lines of democratic accountability".

"We won't unlock New Zealand's potential while the political and judicial classes experiment on our basic rights," Seymour said.

"Inventing new legal concepts, dividing us according to some people's version of history and trampling our property rights might be fun for wig wearers in court and lanyard wearers in the public service, but all it does for the ordinary person is created uncertainty and frustration."

Speaking to RNZ, Te Pāti Māori co-leader Debbie Ngārewa-Packer compared the policy to the Treaty Principles Bill and said Aotearoa had already sent a "very clear" message about it - Hikoi mō Te Tiriti.

"The very government he's in didn't support it, and there's millions of dollars wasted when we've got a nation that's dealing with a cost of living crisis, a fuel crisis, and an opportunity loss crisis.

"What we should be doing is having a government and parties that indicate their willingness to take the country forward and not have this nonsense.

"Show me an instance where a house, a farm, [or] public access has been denied because of the Treaty - it just can't be validated." she said.

Ngārewa-Packer accused Seymour of "dog whistling" and creating a "drama that doesn't exist".

"There's a lot of work to do, there's a lot of maturing to do, but again, Māori are not in the way of the progress of Aotearoa."

World.title: National promises no new taxes if re-elected
World.content:
The National Party is promising no new taxes if re-elected this November, but has not ruled out increasing existing taxes.

The party had already ruled out a bank tax and on Sunday scrapped the idea of an accommodation levy on short-term rentals such as bed and breakfasts.

It comes after Prime Minister Christopher Luxon spoke publicly a fortnight ago about the possibility of three new taxes under National - a bed tax, a bank tax, and a fuel excise increase.

The announcement on Sunday ruled out the first two but was silent on the third, fuel excise.

Finance spokesperson Nicola Willis said policies like a bed tax would only hurt those booking weekends away and the party would instead look at existing mechanisms to help councils cope with tourism costs.

She said the party would continue to invest in front-line services and while National was committed to no additional taxes, she said the Labour Party had left the door open to introducing more than its proposed capital gains tax.

Leader Christopher Luxon said taxes would be a "defining theme" of the election.

"Our promise of no new taxes this election reflects our disciplined economic management, focused on growing the economy, creating jobs, lifting wages and keeping taxes low.

"It's part of National's plan to fix the basics and build the future."

Speaking at the policy announcement and the launch of his own Botany campaign, Luxon said National were "committed to the problem" of high tourism costs, but a bed tax was not the solution.

"We couldn't find a way to do it through an accommodation levy, that would end up hurting everyday Kiwis who are just going away for a weekend in Auckland or Queenstown."

Luxon pointed the finger at Labour and "its mates", which he said would see the introduction of up to nine new taxes.

"We are not introducing a capital gains tax, we're not introducing a wealth tax, an inheritance tax, a gift tax, a 45 percent increase to the income tax, a $5 billion tax on businesses, an increase in business tax rates, and the list goes on and on and on.

"That is not happening," he said.

At Budget 2026 in May, Willis - as finance minister - announced a levy on banks which she said would gather about $200 million over for years.

Willis said she had looked at what banks were currently being taxed and what the "measures" to change that were, but could not find "other measures" that would not result in "additional costs" for Kiwis.

"My concern that there isn't a mechanism that won't end up being borne by everyday people on their mortgage or their bank fees - and I don't want that.

"I'm really concerned that Kiwis not face the cost of additional taxes, and while we looked at alternative mechanisms, none of them stacked up against the simple rule: no more costs for Kiwis," she said.

Asked if National meant no increases existing taxes, levies or fees, Willis did not rule it out.

"We're saying no new taxes." she said.

Luxon said the petrol tax had been a "feature of New Zealand's system for decades" and his government had decided not to increase it in their first term.

"We also need to acknowledge that is the way that we actually fund and invest in our roads as well. But this is about no new taxes, and I can't be clearer, this is the fundamental choice of this election.

"You've seen a Labour Party that wants to spend more, they want to tax more, and they want to borrow more, versus responsible economic management that actually grows an economy and improves affordability for all New Zealanders and stops Labour's tax grab," he said.

Asked how the policy would be received by his coalition partners, Luxon said all three parties signed up to lowering taxes for working New Zealanders.

"It was the first thing we did: first tax relief for New Zealanders in 14 years. All parties signed up for that."

Pushed again on if it the no new tax policy would be "solidified" in a potential coalition agreement, Luxon said it would be.

In a statement, Labour's campaign chair Kieran McAnulty said voting for National meant voting for more cuts.

"If you're ruling out revenue, you have to cut spending. So what are you going to cut?

"More nurses? More hospital services? More front-line workers? More support for families?"

McAnulty said New Zealanders had a right to know what "National is planning to take away from them".

"Putting everything on the chopping block is not responsible government," he said.

In response, Willis attacked Labour's newly released fiscal strategy, which looks to hold Crown expenditure at 33 percent of GDP.

World.title: Man in critical condition after being hit by car in Manawatū
World.content:
A man is in critical condition in Wellington Hospital, after being being hit by a car in Manawatū in the early hours of Saturday morning.

He was found after police were called to Halcombe Road, north of Feilding, about 12:20am.

"That person was located with extensive injuries, and is currently in the intensive care unit at Wellington Hospital," Detective David Burrows said.

"The vehicle allegedly involved in this incident left the scene before police arrival - we want to speak with the driver as the information that he has will be vital to our investigation."

Police said there may be witnesses with video footage who were reluctant to come forward.

"There were a number of people in attendance at the time this incident took place, and we believe someone will either have information that can assist us in identifying the alleged driver or any other information that can assist in our investigation," Burrows said.

"We're providing the family of the young person who was injured with the support they need at this time. We're urging people to please consider them and do the right thing and come forward with any information you have."

It was a traumatic incident that "could have so easily been avoided", police said.

"Anti-social road activity is extremely dangerous, whether you are taking part or simply just observing, and this incident should be a reminder of that."

Anyone with information should contact police on 105 by phone or online at 105.police.govt.nz.

Information can also be provided anonymously through Crime Stoppers on 0800 555 111.

World.title: Mediawatch: Are we getting more ‘media mature’?
World.content:
Political twitch on taxing big tech, maturing media Kiwis Mediawatch Download MP3 36m

For years it's been a global mega-trend few media companies could buck - people drawn away in droves from TV, radio and publications by unlimited digital stuff online.

Much of it is fun and free stuff on the likes of YouTube, Facebook and TikTok, fed by billions of users. Fast-proliferating subscription video on demand (SVOD) services have also offered high-quality shows and movies to those prepared to pay a premium.

The biggest survey of news consumption in the world - the Digital News Report 2026 - found social media and video platforms overtook media organisations' own channels this year as the most popular source of information.

While a majority in all 48 countries watched online news video, consumption of video on publishers' own sites and apps fell by five per cent in a year.

As well as the existing audience thinning out, local media face the prospect of following generations never coming to them in numbers. According to the UK's regulator Ofcom, less than a quarter of what 16 to 24 year-olds watch at home comes from broadcasters.

It's not so different here.

"Young people get their news and entertainment from YouTube, Tiktok and Instagram - not Stuff, the Herald and RNZ. Young people thought locally-made content was cringe . . . but a lot of the time, young people didn't know it even existed," The Detail reported in 2023 just after NZ On Air released research on the media habits of 15-24 year-olds.

NZ On Air's bi-annual surveys of people over 15 -

Where are the Audiences? - have also tracked the declining reach of established home-grown media here.

Empire strikes back?

Theo David as Vili in Shortland Street. Supplied / South Pacific Pictures

But two years ago, WATA? 2024 had better news for local media.

"The year-on-year growth of global media platform audiences in New Zealand appears to be slowing - while the decline for local platforms may be stabilising," NZ On Air said at the time.

"We are still engaging with local [media] despite the fact that we are moving more to global and digital," Glasshouse media's Amanda Wisnewski told Mediawatch at the time.

The just-released WATA? 2026 report shows the empire striking back again. The new surveyor Verian concluded "established and emerging platforms increasingly coexist rather than replace one another".

TV broadcasters reached more New Zealanders each day - live and on-demand - than global video platforms, according to the survey of 1700 people in April and May 2026.

Radio is still strong in the mornings, with more people going online and streaming later in the day - and there's an uptick in TV broadcasts in the traditional evening peaktimes too.

News articles (either online or hardcopy) reached over half of New Zealanders.

Fewer of us shelling out for Netflix, Spotify and the rest

Local media - and free platforms - may be benefitting from the cost of living cutting the appeal of streaming services offering premium content for a price. NZ On Air 'Where are the Audiences 2026' survey

Netflix surged after it finally arrived in New Zealand in 2014. By 2020, the WATA? survey found 40 percent of Kiwis using it.

But WATA? 2024 found Netflix used by only 38 percent of us - and fewer New Zealanders paying for SVOD across the board - while 60 percent watched New Zealand TV channels in 2024 for an average of three-and-a-half hours a day, either live or on-demand.

This year, that's up again to 63 percent, and more than one-in-three people surveyed used New Zealand-based broadcast video on-demand (BVOD) such as TVNZ+, ThreeNow and SkyGo daily.

The cost-of-living crisis and rising subscription fees have accelerated SVOD's retreat.

Netflix daily use has dropped to 32 percent. Spotify use is at 27 percent in 2026, down 8 percent since 2024.

This year's survey found 62 percent using global video-sharing platforms daily, with 15-39 year-olds, Māori, Pacific and Asian people heavier than average users.

YouTube now reaches more than half of New Zealanders daily (52 percent), but so does TVNZ (53 per cent) and it is well ahead of other sources of online viewing, and the biggest social platform Facebook.

Four years ago, the survey found almost two out of three people aged 40-59 were using YouTube, and over-60s were going online at record rates too.

Local content in the media mix

Encouraging numbers for local content in NZ on Air's latest 'Where are the Audiences?' survey. supplied

NZ On Air will be heartened by the survey finding local content is widely seen as high quality and that people who have watched local shows recently value them more.

"Most New Zealanders believe NZ music matches international quality, while many also see NZ shows as comparable to overseas content. Both NZ music and NZ shows are strongly associated with national pride," says Verian in WATA? 2026.

"I suspect more and more New Zealanders see our broadcasters as safe havens - delivering familiar fare and greater relevance with local programming," New Zealand Herald editor turned media researcher Dr Gavin Ellis wrote this week.

He believed WATA? 2026 showed local broadcasters "back on top" in a fragmented market, and also highlighted better results for local content.

"Almost half of the sample recently watched a New Zealand-made show. The ratio was even higher among people aged over 60. Almost two-thirds of those surveyed thought local quality was as good as overseas content and 71 per cent said that content made them "a little prouder to be a New Zealander".

But the picture is different when you break the population down, as NZ on Air did with separate survey reports on younger people, Māori (PDF), Pacific (PDF, and Asian New Zealanders (PDF).

These found the global platforms still sit at the centre of young people's media habits.

Māori use most of the same platforms as the wider population, but Netflix is bigger for them - and Facebook use is up there with YouTube.

The platforms Pacific audiences use "most reflect a digital-first and social media ecosystem", the survey concluded. And the likes of YouTube, Instagram and TikTok dominated Asian New Zealanders' daily media habits - and captured more of their time than any other media activity.

These parts of our population are also among the fastest-growing, so can local media keep on clawing back overall attention as recorded in the national surveys?

Dilemma for NZ On Air

Cameron Harland of NZ on Air Copyright 2013

WATA? 2026 also raises questions for NZ On Air. Are people getting the local content they fund, given the ever-increasing range of outlets New Zealanders use? And do they like what they find?

The survey found two-thirds of people can find NZ content easily, though more people said they find out about them via social media - and fewer are alerted by promos on TV.

"I think we're seeing free and paid, local and global, traditional and digital media coexisting rather than simply replacing one another," NZ On Air chief executive Cameron Harland told Mediawatch.

While the reach of Netflix and Spotify was down, the people who are paying for it were using it more. People were also spending more time listening to podcasts, radio and music streaming.

"That's probably one of the fundamental findings from the research. There's not a lot of new customers finding their way into different places, but those that are engaging are engaging for longer - pretty much across the board."

Are local and free platforms getting the benefit of the rising cost-of-living?

"I suspect that there is a little bit of that. I think a little more about if I need to have all of these streaming platforms at the same time. But we're moving into a more sophisticated viewing environment in the way that people are engaging with the many options available."

If the economy improves, could that flip back? People may start spending on offshore platforms' subscriptions again, undermining the domestic media outlets NZ On Air needs to air the content it funds.

"Possibly. But you could say that our local platforms are doing a good job. TVNZ+ is a fantastic streaming platform. ThreeNow is the same."

"They're investing massively in their streaming infrastructure, and the content. The FIFA World Cup went well for TVNZ, but it's also a great opportunity for them to get (more) viewers to the platform and they can cross-promote other content."

Will this change what NZ On Air spends our money on?

"There's a couple of examples in recent years where we have made some tangible changes based upon the findings that we've seen from the research," Harland told Mediawatch.

One is the 2023 youth content strategy Within My Reach (PDF), which states bluntly: "Our research has highlighted that 15 - 24-year-olds have largely disengaged from traditional media platforms, such as television, and are increasingly turning to social media and international streaming services as their primary sources of content."

NZ On Air also funded a recent series about social media mental health aimed at younger people - Under the Influence.

In the past it would have been a TV documentary made for TVNZ or TV3's weekday peaktime. But UTI was broken up into 15-minute episodes on the New Zealand Herald website and also posted on YouTube where it was more likely to reach younger people.

"Those youth-orientated pieces of work need to be where they are. We have a strategy that does allow for that content to go digital-first sort of into social media and also hoping that there might be secondary plays into TVNZ or 3Now or other places."

But if local linear and on-demand TV is edging out the share of the global video sharing platforms, will NZ On Air go back to the future and spend more big money on more productions for television?

"We are definitely not shying away from putting serious investment into primetime shows. That kind of the peak-time TV content is still very much kind of supported by us and delivering significant audiences," said Harland.

"That youth content going into YouTube and the global video players is still a relatively modest level of funding that we're putting in."

For decades, Shortland Street was funded by TVNZ itself from advertising revenue the show attracted in TVNZ2 at 7pm on weekdays.

Now $2.3 million a year goes into the production - described by NZ on Air as a 'life-saving injection' - and it also qualifies for the Screen Production Rebate.

"On one level it's frustrating that we're having to fund something that we didn't need to fund previously," Cameron Harland told Mediawatch.

"But that is also just simply the nature of the commercial environment the broadcasters exist within. The audience for that show is actually significant and relatively young, which are those that are quite hard to find."

Ms. X - funded by NZ on Air - starring Australian actor Melissa George. supplied

$8m was recently devoted to four scripted projects, including Ms. X (on Three right now, starring Australian actor Melissa George) and the return of local comedy Wellington Paranormal.

Reality shows Celebrity Treasure Island and The Traitors - both versions of proven hit international franchises - are funded by NZ On Air too.

"I think most people are acknowledging that it is a tough media environment for these platforms to fund this content themselves. We feel like we have data on our side. We really understand whether audiences are engaging in this content or not - and the fact that they are is really important.

"To a certain extent, our life is about tension. We have a requirement to fund content for a number of different audiences that are listed in our Act.

"Most of our content is still being funded into New Zealand-owned broadcast platforms - by some significant margin. The local platforms are by far and away the best place for the content to sit because they are doing a really good job in promoting it in the really fragmented media landscape that we now operate in."

Partnership with platforms

AFP / NurPhoto / Samuel Boivin

NZ On Air raised eyebrows in the media when it partnered with Netflix on a programme - Toi Atea - to fast-track people into screen production.

Netflix carries few local productions and rarely invests in any. Aren't domestic broadcasters better placed to train and employ people here?

"What you're also hearing, no doubt, is people saying Netflix is not engaging in commissioning local content. Let's get them around the table and have some good conversations about what's going on.

"Netflix have put money into this programme. In turn we are selecting local productions for people to work on - and that the money is paying for those people to engage in that.

"The local productions are . . . for the most part . . . shows that are going to be playing into local platforms. Netflix have just come along and said they are keen to support us financially in this.

"We'd be more than happy for TVNZ or Sky/Three or RNZ to support us financially in this as well.

World.title: Otago oncology professor calls ACT's cancer centre policy 'magical thinking'
World.content:
ACT's proposal to build a national cancer centre is being labelled a fantasy by an oncology professor.

The party is turning Paul Henry's idea of building a dedicated, centralised cancer facility, into policy, recently unveiling a plan to build a "Starship for Cancer" with campuses in Auckland and Christchurch.

ACT expected around $2 billion of capital investment would be required, with funding from public-private partnerships, donations, and existing Crown health investment.

It also planned to establish a philanthropic foundation to attract some of the funding, and get rid of a cap on donation tax credits.

ACT is campaigning for a dedicated national cancer centre, after Paul Henry put the idea forward. RNZ

But philanthropic funding was "magical thinking," according to University of Otago professor of cancer medicine, Chris Jackson, who said overseas models were typically funded by private patients.

He said while it was easy enough to raise money for a building, securing funding for an ongoing service was an entirely different challenge.

"Cancer care operational expenditure year by year, ongoing, is hundreds of millions of dollars, if not more.

"The idea of getting that amount of money from philanthropy year, on year, on year, is just magical thinking."

Jackson, who is married to Labour MP Rachel Brooking, said there was a raft of ways to invest in cancer care, that in his opinion, should be prioritised over a large cancer hospital.

"First off the rank, would be a lung cancer screening programme which would meaningfully improve cure rates in lung cancer," he said.

"The next thing we could do is lower the ... screening age for bowel cancer. I don't see philanthropists lining up to fund that, either."

Jackson said New Zealand had a problem with access to cancer diagnoses, with one of the highest rates of late diagnosis among comparable countries.

He said early diagnosis was done in the regions and was adamant a central cancer facility would only exacerbate the current issues - by draining those areas of much-needed resources.

"This proposal is going to do nothing to help the person with bowel cancer in Invercargill, with breast cancer in Timaru, or prostate cancer in Gisborne.

"Those are the sorts of people who will miss out under this type of policy."

Jackson said New Zealand needed a structure that enabled people to receive cancer treatment close to home.

World.title: Officials keep quiet after botched Lake Alice compensation
World.content:
MSD doesn't say if it's checking Lake Alice torture survivors' benefit decisions after compensation botch up

The agency wrongly denied accommodation supplement to a Lake Alice survivor, but the decision was overturned

Former human rights commissioner criticises MSD's stance.

Officials are not saying if they've checked to make sure survivors of torture at the notorious Lake Alice child and adolescent unit haven't wrongly had benefits cut because of compensation they've received.

RNZ reported last month that Paul Zentveld, who has a King's Service Medal for services to survivors of abuse in care, was unable to pay his rent and was living in his house bus in a public car park after his accommodation supplement was cancelled when it shouldn't have been.

Zentveld is one of more than 100 Lake Alice survivors who opted for a $150,000 compensation payment for torture suffered during the 1970s at the unit, overseen by Dr Selwyn Leeks. Others have negotiated settlements through arbitration.

Ministry of Social Development rules say compensation for Lake Alice survivors or assets they've bought with compensation money should not be considered when they're assessed for benefit entitlements.

Yet a boat worth about $23,000 Zentveld bought with his money was wrongly ruled to mean he was ineligible for receiving accommodation supplement payments, a decision reversed when he successfully appealed to the MSD's benefits review committee.

Lake Alice survivor forced to live in car after accomodation supplement cancelled Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

MSD doesn't say if it has reviewed other decisions

Zentveld is concerned other Lake Alice survivors in his situation would also be affected.

RNZ has spoken with another survivor who was also denied their accommodation supplement due to an asset they'd bought using their compensation money, only for the decision to be reversed after Zentveld's story was reported.

MSD's group manager for client service delivery Graham Allpress said he couldn't comment on individual cases without a privacy waiver, but said it regularly reviewed decisions.

"If we get something wrong, we want to make it right as quickly as possible.

"Many of our staff have been working with survivors of abuse for a long time. They work hard to provide people with the support they're entitled to."

RNZ asked if MSD would check with all Lake Alice survivors who had received compensation to make sure their benefit entitlements weren't wrongly affected.

Allpress said MSD had "specific operational guidance which applies to Lake Alice survivors and their compensation payments".

Lake Alice Hospital PUBLIC DOMAIN./ Pawful

"We also provide more detailed guidance to MSD staff about how to support survivors who come to us for assistance. This includes both survivors of abuse in general, and Lake Alice survivors specifically.

"We've sent updates to every MSD staff member nationwide about our work on historic claims, including Lake Alice compensation payments and how they interact with other types of MSD assistance."

MSD historic claims staff received an overview of the Royal Commission into abuse in state and faith care, and updates on progress against its redress implementation plan.

Allpress referred RNZ to its guidance for assessing Lake Alice survivors who had received compensation, which is published online.

The section dealing with survivors' "cash asset levels" doesn't specifically say assets are excluded from calculations when benefits are assessed, saying: "Note for this exemption, cash means physical cash and money in the bank (including savings and term deposit accounts). It does not include anything purchased with the payment, such as shares."

RNZ sought further clarification.

Allpress said this was the current guidance for staff.

"As previously advised, decisions of the benefits review committee only apply to a client's individual case. They do not set a precedent. The [committee] decision is being considered as part of ongoing work around redress payments and the welfare system," he said.

"We encourage anyone has concerns about decisions we have made to contact us. They can challenge it and it can be reviewed."

A memorial to Lake Alice victims was unveiled earlier this year. RNZ/Jimmy Ellinghm

No apology amid reversal

Zentveld has since received a letter saying his accommodation supplement will be restored and arrears paid. It did not include an apology.

He was concerned that MSD did not say if it would check to make sure other survivors weren't affected as he was, and said decisions about their entitlements should be reviewed to ensure they complied with the rules exempting Lake Alice compensation money and purchases from that.

"Why should they have to individually fight it? This is what the Royal Commission is worried about."

Zentveld said there seemed to be a lack of accountability.

Former chief human rights commissioner David Rutherford, who has supported Zentveld's fight for recognition for abuse survivors for years, including to the United Nations Committee against Torture, was also concerned, saying MSD should check to make sure others weren't affected.

"The social agencies are behaving as if they just want to be left alone to get on with business as usual."

World.title: Hospital security appeared powerless against 'intimidating' patient, witness says
World.content:
A woman who waited more than eight hours in a hospital emergency department says security officers appeared powerless to stop a man intimidating other patients.

The woman, who asked not to be named, arrived at the Palmerston North Hospital ED about 3pm on 28 July.

The man was escorted in by police about 11pm, who then left the scene, she said. The man behaved poorly, getting in people's faces, vaping, crashing into a wall and writhing on the ground, she said.

The man appeared to have come to the emergency department because of a sore shoulder, she said.

"He was just being really weird and intimidating, and walking up to people and staring at them in the eyes, then walking on to the next person.

"There were a number of older people and people with little babies in there, and he didn't seem to care about that," she said.

He was physically intimidating due to his size, she added.

"Everyone was just avoiding this guy's gaze, really, like you would if you had a scary dog."

The woman said two or three security officers were keeping an eye on the man, but were not intervening.

At present they can only calm situations without using force.

Emergency Department security guards deal with increase in physical and verbal abuse Morning Report Download MP3 5m

"He just felt like someone who at any point could give someone a big whack on the head. He was also really out of it," the woman told RNZ.

"It was just really surprising to me that anyone like that was allowed to stay in that space and they weren't asked to leave."

The man was there for about 30 minutes before he went to the department desk and demanded to be seen. Despite many others having waited for hours, the man was attended to by medical staff.

"I really felt for the medical team, because it was like, 'let's just get this guy out of the way, this volatile person, and let's just treat him'.

"But that just creates this sort of feeling that you come in, you behave terribly, you're intimidating, and then you get looked after. Meanwhile, there are other people who are patiently waiting."

The woman said she would like to see hospital security given more power to remove people from hospital property when they behave as the man did.

RNZ has previously reported calls for beefed up powers for security officers amid growing instances of violence and intimidation at hospitals, although some in the health sector say such moves could be problematic.

The Post reported this week that Health NZ is planning on spending up to $100 million on improved security in hospitals.

Health NZ says security staff and clinical teams are trained in calming and de-escalation techniques. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Poor behaviour not tolerated - Health NZ

RNZ contacted Health NZ about the incident. Included in our questions was what should happen in such situations, was this incident reported by staff and had officials considered giving hospital security more powers.

Health NZ's interim group director of operations for MidCentral, Katherine Fraser-Chapple, said patient safety was the organisation's highest priority.

"We want everyone who attends Palmerston North Hospital to feel safe and supported while receiving care," she said.

"We do not tolerate behaviour that causes distress, intimidation or risk to patients, visitors, or staff.

"Health New Zealand has processes in place to manage disruptive or concerning behaviour, including support from security staff and clinical teams trained in calming and de-escalation techniques."

Fraser-Chapple said where appropriate, security staff would work alongside police "to help maintain a safe environment for everyone in our care".

World.title: Labour releases fiscal strategy, promises to slash debt
World.content:
Labour has released their fiscal strategy for the election, promising to get back to surplus by 2029/30, slash debt and set up an independent Parliamentary Budget Office, if elected.

Leader Chris Hipkins said his party would "get the books back into shape", but would not do it by "making life harder" and cutting services.

"New Zealand should be a country where hard work gets you somewhere. Where you can get ahead, put down roots and know your kids will have opportunities here.

"We'll invest in the things that make New Zealand stronger - our hospitals and schools, infrastructure, skills and the businesses that create jobs" Hipkins said.

Labour's fiscal strategy has six policies:

Achieve a surplus by 2029/30 and keep a sustainable fiscal position over the forecast period. Labour return to using the original OBEGAL (Operating Balance Before Gains and Losses) indicator and ditch the OBEGALx measure introduced by Finance Minister Nicola Willis.

Aim to reduce net debt down to 20 percent of GDP over time and investment in initiatives that support a growing economy.

Keep core Crown Expenditure and revenue at around 33 percent of GDP when their capital gains tax is fully implemented.

Set up an independent Parliamentary Budget Office to scrutinise government finances and election commitments.

Give the Reserve Bank it's dual mandate back, making so it must consider price stability and maximum sustainable employment.

And, bring back wellbeing reporting to so decisions take into account the impact on New Zealanders.

Finance and economy spokesperson Barbara Edmonds said the plan would balance the books and bring down debt, while giving New Zealand the "capacity to invest in its future".

"Labour will return the books to surplus by 2029/30 and reduce net debt over time but we won't do that by cutting the foundations of our economy."

Finance and economy spokesperson Barbara Edmonds and Labour leader Chris Hipkins. Baz Macdonald/RNZ

"Under National unemployment is at an 11-year high, business liquidations are up 71 percent, homelessness and KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals are at record levels, and public services are under pressure - that isn't economic success," Edmonds said.

Edmonds told media at the policy announcement in Wellington that a more detailed fiscal plan would be laid out once the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update (PREFU) was outlined.

"The pre-election fiscal update is really important for us to show our debt trajectory as part of our fiscal plan... [that's] the reason why we want it [debt] at 20 percent, around a prudent level. It allows for buffers for economic shocks. "

"We saw that in previous years when Labour brought back the books into surplus. We had to put the umbrella up when we were faced with a 1-in-100-year pandemic. That's why debt levels can change because of extra conditions that the government has no control over." she said.

Edmonds said expenditure would be "be a little bit higher" under her party's plan because of the investments they planned to make in areas like healthcare.

"With the CGT, revenue increases over time, that's what you see in overseas jurisdictions."

"So for us, we bring the legislation, and then obviously as the years progress... it does increase over time." she said.

Hipkins said Labour was "always" looking for better ways to spend taxpayer money.

"There are some changes in the medium to longer term we're seeing in education, for example, [where] we have the opposite trajectory to the one we're seeing in aged care."

"There's actually going to be fewer kids coming through the education system. [and] that's going to open up some choices about what we do there."

The government has recently signed a public-private partnership (PPP) agreement to build the first section of the Northland Expressway between Warkworth and Te Hana.

Asked what Labour would do to fund infrastructure projects, Hipkins said that was a "subject of considerable debate across the house".

"We do need more stability in the infrastructure pipeline, and that includes a more mature conversation about how we fund that over the medium to longer term."

"A lot of the projects that the National Party have been announcing around the country, they haven't identified how they're going to pay for them yet." he said.

Hipkins had a message for his potential coalition partners.

"Voters should get the sort of government that they vote for, and if New Zealanders vote for Labour to lead the next government, this is the sort of economic management approach that we're going to be taking." he said.

Speaking on introducing an independent Parliamentary Budget Office, Edmonds said she wanted the position to be an "officer of Parliament", meaning the position agreed to unanimously and with bipartisan support.

"However, Treasury also looked at other particular options where it becomes like a unit of treasury, for example. But the ideal option is to try to get that bipartisanship because it benefits all New Zealanders."

Edmonds said the Australian model was something she "looked at closely" and she had a members bill that sought to replicate that model.

On well-being reporting, Edmonds said they would be introduced through an amendment to the Public Finance Act and would provide a "fuller understanding" of how fiscal decision impacted on the wellbeing of New Zealanders.

Asked about giving the Reserve Bank a dual mandate to consider price stability and employment, Hipkins said it was "hardly radical".

"The Australians have one, the Americans have one. Many other countries around the world have the same objective." he said.

Edmonds said using the OBEGAL, as opposed to OBEGALx, would provide "certainty".

"OBEGAL is quite an internationally well-used measure, used by credit reporting agencies and other governments. We're providing that certainty that we want to keep Obi-Gal and not just make up a new measure to exclude ACC."

'Exploding debt and economic vandalism' - National

In a statement, National's finance spokesperson Nicola Willis said Labour's strategy amounted to nothing more than "spending more, borrowing more and taxing more".

National's finance spokesperson Nicola Willis RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"[It's] the same approach that led New Zealand into the sky-high inflation, exploding debt and economic vandalism Labour imposed on Kiwis last time."

"Targeting revenue at 33 percent of GDP means that by 2031, Labour would need to be collecting an additional $10.3 billion in revenue every year - far more than the $1.35 billion they say their capital gains tax will raise in that same year."

She said the proposal to "water down" the Reserve Bank's inflation targets risked "rising prices for every Kiwi".

"Tellingly, Labour has not made clear in their fiscal rules announcement that their new Capital Gains Tax is the only tax change they would implement, leaving the door open to a suite of further tax changes."

"Before the 2020 election, Labour ruled out the Ute Tax, changes to the bright-line tax and changes to interest deductibility - then implemented all three after the election. And it's growing clearer by the day that Labour is planning the same thing if elected on 7 November." she said.

Around two weeks ago the National Party released its own so-called Budget Responsibility Rules which Finance spokesperson Nicola Willis described as "fiscal guard-rails" and leader Christopher Luxon said would protect the country against economic shocks.

National said it would return to surplus in 2028/29 - under its OBEGALx formula - but would hit surplus the same year as Labour is projecting under the OBEGAL measure.

National would also keep Crown expenditure down towards 30 percent of GDP and get debt down to below 40 percent of GDP.

ACT Leader David Seymour said Hipkins was "going back to the future".

ACT Leader David Seymour RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

"Higher taxes, higher spending, more complicated monetary policy, and another empty promise that somehow it will all add up."

"He has promised billions of spending to tickle every electoral itch, but today is promising to spend less with no explanation how other than more taxes that don't come close to paying for his promises."

He said restoring the Reserve Ba k's dual mandate was an "Ardern-era" policy.

"The Reserve Bank is meant to be laser-focused on reining in inflation. Adding a second "jobs" target, totally at odds with the inflation target, will mean a higher cost of living for New Zealanders."

World.title: 'Mainly to support AFLW': Swans fans descend on SCG amid club scandal
World.content:
Sydney Swans supporter Teri turned up to the SCG with a homemade sign reading: "I'm here for the AFLW".

"[I'm here] mainly to support AFLW women in light of everything that's happened. They still need our support," Teri said.

"I still love the game and I still love Sydney, just extremely disappointed."

Sydney Swans play after Pullman Hotel scandal Sydney's AFLW team takes the field in the first game of a double-header, with some fans threatening to walk out on the following men's game. Follow live.

She is one of many fans who have descended on the SCG ahead of the historic double-header between the men's and women's teams. It comes in an emotional week as a scandal continues to engulf the club.

Five players — Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon — have been stood down by the Swans for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late following last Sunday's win over Essendon in Melbourne.

Police from Victoria's sexual crimes squad are separately investigating a report of sexual assault, which the ABC understands centres on a player allegedly touching a woman without her consent.

Police have not made any arrests or laid charges.

Swans fans arrive at the SCG ahead of the historic double-header. (Getty: Cameron Spencer)

Teri, a decades-long supporter of the club, expressed great disappointment.

"As a fan, as a decades supporter, always thinking this club was something better, raising up against racism, like back to Goodsey … I thought they were much better than this," she said.

"It's hard to be proud at the moment."

She said she would play it by ear whether she stays for the men's game.

"It's got nothing to do with the women, and I think they are suffering as well … these are people they thought were their friends," Teri said.

"It was important for me to make sure that I came out for the women, wear my women's AFLW merch, so that's the first thing and I'll decide as I'm there because I also feel for the remainder of the team, the men's team."

There was talk during the week of a fan boycott of the men's game, where some fans have decided to show up for the AFLW game between Sydney and Essendon and leave before the men's Swans team run out against North Melbourne.

Swans spectators arrive for the AFLW match between Sydney Swans and Essendon Bombers at the SCG. (Gett6y: Cameron Spencer)

For long-term fan and member Meagan Masters, the past week has left her "gutted", saying the image of the "wholesome" club had been shattered.

"I feel like I know the players, and so just disappointment and really heartbroken for the other members of the team at this stage in the competition where they were heading possibly to a flag," she told the ABC as she made her way to the SCG.

She said the alleged actions of the five players was "unacceptable" for professional athletes, and she was "100 per cent" behind their ban for the remainder of the season, but said she was keeping an open mind because no-one knows exactly what happened at the hotel.

Meagan Masters says this week has left her "gutted" and "heartbroken". (ABC News: Patrick Thomas)

Ms Masters, who regularly goes to both the men's and women's games, said she expected a large turnout today.

"I think we're going to get that record crowd that we're after," she said.

" I love the girls, I love the boys and I think they're still going to be banded as a club. Just five guys doesn't define a club. The Swans are more than that. "

Fans grapple with Swans scandal Sydney Swans fans are grappling with an emotional week of developments ahead of a historic double-header, as a scandal continues to engulf the team.

David Lipman also there to support the women's team, agreed that fans would turn out in droves.

"They've [women's team] done nothing wrong," he said.

"They may feel that what's alleged to have occurred is detrimental to their standing, but the rest of the club are supporting them and they deserve it."

Swans fans queue up to enter ahead of Sydney's AFLW match against Essendon. (Getty: Cameron Spencer)

Chris Lewis goes to most AFLW games in New South Wales and came out in a GWS pride kit to support the AFLW game today.

"[I'm feeling] incredibly disappointed. There is no doubt about that it's been probably the worst week for NSW footy that we have ever had," he said.

"It's been horrible, it's been horrible as a parent to young kids, trying to explain this stuff when they were fans of some of the players involved. It's just been an absolute awful week for all footy fans in NSW."

Chris Lewis came out to support the Sydney Swans AFLW side at the SCG. (702 ABC Sydney: Georgie Carroll)

On whether he would stay for the men's match, similar to Teri he said he would play it by ear, but likely would not stay.

"I've been trying to weigh this up all week. I'm a big fan of the North Melbourne men's team, especially Cooper Trembath, but I'll probably be leaving. It just doesn't seem appropriate, it doesn't seem right to stay," he said.

World.title: Bristol City striker's stunning backheel goal in England goes viral
World.content:
Bristol City striker Dom Ballard scored an outrageous backheel volley against Birmingham in the Championship overnight, sparking social media users to suggest the goal of the year race may already be over.

With his back to goal, Ballard connected his heel perfectly with a Rio Cardines cross to send the ball flying into the top corner and give his side the lead in the 85th minute.

Birmingham would go on to score from the penalty spot to end the game in a draw, but all the talk was about Ballard's stunning goal.

"The fans were amazing and I ran straight to them when I scored which was an incredible feeling," Ballard said.

"I won't score many better than that."

The goal saw the term Puskás Award trending on X, as users suggested the race for the best goal of the season was already done and dusted.

Despite the stunning effort, Ballard said he was disappointed with the result.

"We are disappointed with the result in the end as I thought we were the better team," he said.

"But everyone played their role well today and when you come to a new club, you want to hit the ground running so to get the goal today against a good Birmingham City side is great."

World.title: Live: Swans fans trickle out of SCG before men's game as women claim victory
World.content:
Sydney's AFLW team has won its game at the SCG in emotional scenes, as a threat of a walkout before the men's match over the scandal that has engulfed the club failed to eventuate in large numbers.

Five men's team players — Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon — have been stood down for breaching team standards.

Several fans outside the SCG said they were torn about whether to walk out before the men's game, while others said they hoped today's games would be a chance to unify the club. One fan had his banner removed by security, while it was confirmed the 16,672 through the gate for the AFLW was a new record for a Swans game.

In Sunday's other AFL games, Essendon lost to Port Adelaide in a heartbreaker at Docklands, looking in their place on the bottom of the ladder, while Hawthorn travels to Perth to face the West Coast Eagles at 7:20pm, with a top four spot on the line for the Hawks.

Follow the live blog below and tune in to our live radio coverage.

World.title: Australia completes innings victory over Bangladesh inside two days in Mackay
World.content:
Australia has wrapped up a dominant victory over Bangladesh inside two days at Mackay's Harrup Park by an innings and 51 runs.

Mitchell Starc was again the destroyer, taking 4-39 to give him 10-51 for the match, his fourth-career 10-wicket match haul in Tests.

The result means the series is tied 1-1 after Bangladesh's historic victory in Darwin last week.

After 18 wickets fell on the first day there was always a possibility that Mackay's Test match debut would be a brief one.

And so it proved, with Shoriful Islam setting the tone with a brilliant inswinging yorker to dismiss Cameron Green for 67.

Australia had resumed on 8-165, with Green and Nathan Lyon adding 21 before Shoriful's phenomenal delivery, which gave him a seventh wicket of the match.

Lyon added 22 to his not-out score overnight, and ended the innings unbeaten on 32 after Josh Hazlewood skied Taijul Islam to Shadman Islam at midwicket.

That gave Australia a total of 210, a lead of 146 at the change of innings.

And after an hour of the Bangladesh innings, the hopes of the tourists getting Australia to bat again already looked faint.

Starc picked up from where he left off in the second innings. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

Starc took two in consecutive balls in his second over to dismiss Shadman Islam (1) and Mominul Haque (0).

Tanzid Hasan (9) also fell before lunch, pulling Cummins to Starc at fine leg, leaving Bangladesh 3-39 at lunch.

After the break, Bangladesh showed little of the resilience and patience that characterised their Darwin display, with skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto throwing his wicket away by chipping Lyon down Starc's throat at long off for 31.

Litton Das picked up his third duck for the series by edging Starc to Webster at third slip, before Pat Cummins prised out Mehidy Hasan Miraz (1) and Hasan Mahmud (2) in consecutive overs.

Starc grabbed his 10th for the match just before tea, bowling Taijul Islam for 7.

After tea, Australia made short work of the last two wickets, Nathan Lyon taking two in four balls to seal the victory and ensure Bangladesh failed to reach 100 in either of their two innings for the first time in a Test match.

It was most fitting that the final wicket was caught by Starc, who was given player of the match and series honours, as the 36-year-old continues his career-best form.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Pogačar hails rival after 'unimaginable' week following brother's death
World.content:
Tadej Pogačar has delivered an ominous and stunning start to the Vuelta a España, edging British rider Ethan Hayter by just 0.09 seconds in the opening stage time trial.

However, the world number one said after the race that he had hoped Britain's Josh Tarling would come out on top.

Tarling was competing in the Vuelta just days after his brother Finlay Tarling was killed when he was hit by a non-accredited car on the course during the Volta a Portugal.

Competing despite his brother's death, Tarling delivered a blistering time of his own to be well in contention for stage honours.

As it happened, Soudal Quick-Step's Hayter finished four seconds faster than his grieving compatriot, with Pogačar pipping them both, before saying it would have been fitting had Tarling claimed victory.

"When I was going to the start line, I saw that Josh has the best time and, I really wish he wins today," Pogačar said at the finish.

"For sure I would do my best, but it was also this kind of strange moment. I was really rooting, myself, for Josh.

"Then I came to the intermediate [time check] and I hear a different name [over the radio], I hear Ethan Hayter was ahead of me by three seconds and I say, 'OK, I give it my all but no risks' and then we'll see what happens.

"I would really like to see Josh do well at this Vuelta."

Tarling's Netcompany INEOS director sportif Geraint Thomas was also full of praise for Tarling.

"It's been great to have him here. He was really keen to ride and wanted to get back to the day job and find comfort in the process and be around the team to be a normal as possible," fellow Welshman Thomas said.

"It's been unimaginable what he's gone through this last week or so.

Josh Tarling was awarded the white jersey as the race's Most Combative Rider after the first stage. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

"To put in a performance like that at the end of the week or so is just fantastic and shows the class of him as person and an athlete, so [we] couldn't be prouder.

"I think the course suited him technically. He's one of the best and yesterday was probably the first time he's ridden a bike properly in a while, so to still put that in is insane, really.

"We'll just continue to be normal around him now and support as best we can."

Tarling's parents, Michael and Dawn, had both given their eldest son their blessing to compete at the Vuelta, saying it was what his brother would have wanted.

"Finlay was so incredibly proud of his big brother, and would be watching, nose to the TV and shouting as he competed," they wrote in a post on social media.

"So it is right that Josh honours that love."

Tarling, for his part, said he was "super happy" with his performance.

"I'm super happy, as happy as I can be," he said.

"I needed to distract myself. Thanks to my family for giving me the blessing to come here and just do another bike race."

Pogačar looking for history

Tadej Pogačar powers through the streets of Monaco to make the perfect start to the Spanish Vuelta. (Getty Images: Laurent Coust/Europa Press)

Pogačar, who's bidding to become just the ninth men's rider to win all three Grand Tours in their career, put himself in position from the offset by completing the highly technical 9.5-kilometre course through the streets of Monaco — where he resides — in 10 minutes, 57 seconds.

Pogačar is competing at the Vuelta for the first time since making his Grand Tour debut as a 20-year-old in the 2019 race. He won three stages and finished third, which incredibly is his worst overall result in the three-week events.

This year is going much better, though.

Why these people believe in 'freak' Pogačar's victories As Tadej Pogačar continues to mop up cycling's biggest accolades and most controversial record, one former doper believes he's found the answer to his success: he is just a "freak".

Pogačar won the Tour de France for the third-straight time to claim his fifth overall title in July, equalling the record for the most overall wins at the race.

The two-time reigning world champion also won the Tour de Suisse and Tour de Romandie stage races as well as celebrating victories at three of the year's one-day monument races — Liège-Bastogne-Liège, the Ronde van Vlaanderen and Milano-Sanremo — while finishing second in the other, Paris-Roubaix.

He also claimed victory in Strade Bianche and has now finished first in 17 of the 38 race days he has completed in 2026.

Pogačar won the Giro d'Italia at the first attempt in 2024, so the Vuelta is the only Grand Tour race he is yet to conquer.

The only other men to have won all three are Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault, Jacques Anquetil, Alberto Contador, Chris Froome, Felice Gimondi, Vincenzo Nibali and his long-time rival, Jonas Vingegaard.

The win was Pogačar's first in the opening stage of a Grand Tour, and it's also the first time he took the red jersey as the Vuelta leader. It's his 36th Grand Tour stage win altogether.

No man has led the Vuelta from start to finish since Swiss legend Tony Rominger did so during the 1994 race.

Such a feat has only happened eight times in men's grand tour history, three times at the Vuelta.

Merckx, the man to whom Pogačar is so often compared, managed the feat once too, at the 1973 Giro d'Italia.

Pogačar's main rival, Vingegaard, is not racing at the 81st edition of the Vuelta as he recovers from a broken collarbone sustained in a crash the day after he was woken at 2am for a doping test at the Tour de France.

Remco Evenepoel, who finished second behind Pogačar at the Tour, is also not competing. The Belgian rider has opted for rest and specific training for the Road World Championships in Montréal next month.

Monaco became the first city to host the start of all three Grand Tours. The Giro d'Italia started in the principality in 1966 and it staged the start of the Tour de France in 2009.

Much of the time trial route on Saturday covered the same course as the annual Formula 1 Grand Prix.

The second stage will also start in Monaco before a 214.3km hilly trek through Provence to Manosque. It will be the longest stage of the race, which finishes in the southern Spanish city of Granada on September 13.

World.title: Teen Socceroo makes perfect EPL debut with win over Manchester United
World.content:
Teenage Socceroo Lucas Herrington has made a dream start to life in the Premier League, coming on as a second-half substitute in Hull City's boilover 2-0 victory over giants Manchester United.

The 18-year-old defender, the only Australian in English soccer's top-flight, didn't put a foot wrong in promoted Hull's return to the big-time when he came on to help them protect their two-goal lead.

The lanky Queenslander was immaculate at the heart of the home side's defence for the final half-hour as Hull confounded all the doubters to earn their first league victory over United in 52 years.

Written off as overwhelming relegation favourites, the Yorkshire side were well worth their win over a lumbering United, whose build-up play was too pedestrian and attacking execution too shoddy.

In the 38th minute the Tigers' central defender Nobel Mendy, who was signed on the same day as Herrington earlier in the month but who got the nod to start ahead of the young Aussie, scored their second goal.

By that time, Michael Carrick's United were already struggling to get to grips with a side that deservedly led through a couple of first-half set-pieces.

Centre-back Semi Ajayi opened the scoring in the 17th minute when United failed to deal with a corner, and then Regan Slater whipped in a 38th minute free-kick that Mendy latched on to, nodding home expertly.

But when Mendy had to come off injured in the 64th minute, Herrington, a record $A33 million signing for an Australian player, got his big moment, the former Colorado Rapids defender coming on in a triple substitution.

He became the first Australian teenager to play in the Premier League since Harry Kewell and, at 18 years 351 days, is the third-youngest Australian to play in England's top-flight.

The youngster with a big reputation for his calmness never looked fazed as United tried to eke their way back into the match with a series of largely lumbering attacks.

He only had nine touches amid United's huff-and-puff but they all told of a lad who already seems at home in this elevated company.

With Hull's Bosnian boss, Sergej Jakirovic, revealing Ajayi, Mendy and captain Lewis Coyle will all have to be assessed for their injuries over the next 24 hours, Herrington will next be in line to feature in Wednesday morning's AEST League Cup tie at Championship side Stoke.

Then he may well feature in their next league game, a huge one at also-promoted Coventry, who lost their opener on Friday 3-0 at champions Arsenal.
